While attempting to cross 13/31, I looked to my right and saw a single engine small aircraft taxiing down Runway 13/31 with a converging path to our aircraft. I called out, 'Stop, Stop, Stop!!' to the Captain, who then brought our aircraft to an abrupt stop in order to avoid collision with the small aircraft. The small aircraft continued to taxi in front of us, right to left without slowing. We stayed put until Ground then again gave us clearance to cross 13/31 S5, T7 to 20C. Ground also apologized to us and said they were not talking to the small aircraft.There was an obvious miscommunication between the small aircraft and Ground, as Ground said, they were not talking to the small aircraft, and the small aircraft stated they had clearance to turn left onto Runway 13/31.
1761615: Approximately 3,000 feet, I was unable to trim nose up. I asked First Officer if he was able to trim nose up. We continue to climb to 5,000 feet, assigned attitude leveled off slowed the aircraft down to 120 knots. We informed ATC we had an issue and wish to remain at 5,000 feet and troubleshoot. We proceeded with the QRH and agreed to perform the Electric Stabilizer Trim Inoperative checklist. We also called Dispatch with the requested link to [Maintenance Control] for further troubleshooting. After counsel with [Maintenance Control] there is no recovery of the pitch trim so we advise dispatch ATC flight attendants and passengers will be returning to ZZZ. We requested RWY XXR and returned for a normal landing. [Report] completed and [Chief Pilot] notified.
1761622: Good rest, day VFR with clear skies throughout the flight. This was the second leg of the day, the first leg being a ferry flight. Uneventful flight. On arrival to the airport we both noticed and mentioned it to each other that ATC left us up a little high. Passing through 15,000 ft. or so and very close to what we thought was the airport. I mentioned 'rather than getting a lot of vectors let's just cancel and make a 360 to the left and go to ZZZZZ, which is the IAF on the RNAV GPS RWY XX), which we did. In no rush, I extended the outbound leg of the 360 turn. Coming out of the turn a little disoriented I asked, 'can you extend the centerline of the runway.' The SIC (Second In Command) which has little time in the plane and not very experienced with the FMS was having trouble putting in the centerline. I asked for a centerline from the RUNWAY, the SIC drew the path from ZZZZZ1, a fix on the approach. The approach is a 45 degree angle from the runway, so when he put the extended line it was from ZZZZZ1 not the runway. I asked again 'I don't think that's right, it doesn't line up.' It was still showing the 45-degree angle to the runway. I again queried him and said, 'What is the runway heading? Make the centerline off that, not any of the fixes.' By then, at around 1000 ft. AGL, we both saw RWY XX painted on the runway in front of us and thought, no worries, I see the numbers.On the landing roll out the chart did not pop up. I asked 'why are we not on the chart? The 350 shows the plane on all the charts'.Reaching the end of the runway the passenger came up and said 'guys, you are at the wrong field, ZZZ is 8 miles south of here, this is ZZZ1' He is a pilot also and was very sympathetic and said 'this happens so often, the operations people don't come out anymore.'I apologized and started planning the trip to ZZZ. I called dispatch and advised them of what happened and what we needed. We taxied back to the approach end of RWY XX and found a place to park and called the FODM (Flight Operations Duty Manager) while the SIC was getting the clearance from ATC. I was told 'he's not answering his phone'. I asked them to 'please find him, I need to talk to him'. A minute or so later [he] answered. I explained what happened. He was very calming and eager to work with me. We talked about the weather, the runway length and width, parachute activity in the area, VFR daytime only airport, he even gave me the frequencies to both airports. Our phones started to beep, at that time [he] said, 'I think they are trying to shut you down, I'll take care of it'. I mentioned that we both had plenty of duty time and felt fine to do the 8-mile flight. It is hard to recall every word but he mentioned something to the effect, 'ok, it looks good, let me check on something, I'll call you back'.After waiting a few minutes and thinking that we had covered everything we needed to for the flight, I decided to depart.The flight to ZZZ was uneventful. The passenger had no problem with the event and being a pilot himself in that area, he kept telling me 'don't worry it really does happen here a lot, ZZZ3 had a RWY XX also. They finally had to change the numbers to XY even though its heading is [different]'. We helped them load their car and they drove off. Things we should/could have done...-Stayed with ATC and gotten better vectors to the airport.-Made sure the centerline was indeed off the runway NOT the FAF.
1761642: Afternoon launch - sort late 90 minutes. My freight recovery specialist, informed me Aircraft X blocked even though the ramp notified the crew to wait for new DG (dangerous goods) paperwork. ACARS was sent to the crew to hold, new DG paperwork on the way. I asked the Captain to call me on the phone to explain that the current DG paper work indicated no DG however, there was IDG (international dangerous goods) onboard and new paperwork is required. We both agreed a block turn back was the best way to handle this situation. Aircraft returned to the blocks for correction of DG paperwork, new release was sent and weight and balance (per Captain's request). Ramp agent made a mistake most likely due to high workload/task saturation and work distractions/interruptions. The sort was over 2 hours late and the load teams were overwhelmed. I had at least 4 adhocs with double legs (out and back) and some with 3 legs. This flight was on hold during most of the sort along with other flights, then decisions were made to reroute the adhocs and add legs. There was a lot of confusion and decisions were being made last minute. We are in unprecedented times. Everyone is doing their best. Some of us are better equipped to handle the constant changes and challenges. Errors will be made, I am glad we were able to correct it and move on.
1761656: On takeoff from PDX, in IMC conditions from takeoff up to about 15,000 ft. MSL. Everything seemed normal until 400 ft. AGL. The captain called 'verify NAV' and I did and then I noticed the EICAS displayed in cyan advisory messages 'Autoland 1 not available' and a second message which I believe was 'RNP (Required Navigation Performance) 0.1 not available.' I am certain about the first message but not about the second. I also noticed that the yellow square with 'RA' was displayed on the PFD in the bottom right corner. This seemed indicative of a radio altimeter malfunction or miscompare. The EICAS messages extinguished quickly and immediately we received an aural warning 'too low, terrain' GPWS message. I did not see a message on the PFD and there was no guidance provided, only the aural warning. I believe the aural warning was only announced once and then went away.This Aural warning is usually only for being low to terrain and not in a correct Landing configuration. We were taking off in takeoff configuration. The gear was up right after takeoff and the flaps were set to 2 for takeoff and had not been retracted since we had not achieved acceleration height. So the aural warning did not make any sense.We both quickly began scanning the instruments and found that the aircraft was already pitched to take off pitch of around 18 degrees nose up. Wings were mostly level. The aircraft was on the flight director. The altitude and vertical speed indicated a climb. Both PFDS displayed the same information. The backup instrument panel displayed the same. The MFD was on terrain display on the map page and showed black terrain in the immediate area and distant green terrain around the aircraft. And thrust was in the TOGA (Takeoff Go Around) position.So everything cross referenced to show a normal, terrain free, take off and climb. Also, we were already in full take off climb thrust, pitch, and configuration. So we continued flight.We got to acceleration height and retracted flaps and continued the remainder of the flight without issue. The issue did not repeat itself again.Another thought is that the IMC conditions were caused by smoke from wild fires. Perhaps the smoke particulates caused a radio altimeter malfunction and the RA briefly read the altitude as too low for only a split second.We were already in GPWS response pitch and configuration. So there was not much else to do. Especially when all indications seemed normal for climb out and the GPWS message was brief and seemed associated with RA malfunction. The only possible extra effort that could be made would be thrust to MAX but that didn't seem necessary in this case as the aural warning had already stopped. The flight departed PDX into immediate IMC because of fog and smoke in the area. Everything was functioning normal and it was standard takeoff and climb. At about 500-600 ft. MSL the FO's (First Officer) PFD indicated an issue with the radar altimeter: amber rectangle with RA. Two EICAS messages appeared. One of them was AUTOLAND 1 NOT AVAIL and I think the second message was something with the RNP (Required Navigation Performance). At which point the EGPWS warning 'TOO LOW, TERRAIN' was heard once. I immediately verified again that the aircraft is pitching up, climbing at takeoff power, on speed, and following the RNAV departure, according to standard profile. Terrain map did not indicate any colors but green and black on the MFD. After a few seconds all messages extinguished and the flight proceeded without any other malfunctions or anomalies.Upon discussing the event with my FO later in cruise, we both thought that it was a radar altimeter anomaly and that the aircraft was at all times operated following normal operating procedures and never outside the normal flight profile/envelope. We also discussed the possibility of an oversized vehicle on the I-205 bridge as that would have been about the point in the air this event occurred.Please monitor if this was a onetime occurrence or there is a trend.
1761664: After takeoff from ZZZ, the red lights for all three landing gear remained illuminated. Accomplished 'landing gear fails to retract' checklist, gear retracted normally, and flight continued to ZZZ1. No airspeed or altitude limits were exceeded. During 'gear fails to retract' checklist, discovered the overhead gear door was slightly open, and after closing it and finishing the checklist, the gear retracted normally. The aircraft was towed to its spot in ZZZ, so the tow team, first officer, and myself all failed to notice the door wasn't completely closed.Will put more emphasis on double checking the configuration of the aircraft after its towed.
1761665: During an ILS approach to Runway XXR, the PF failed to slow early enough on final approach. PF configured later than desired considering the situation (fast due to earlier ATC request) resulting in the aircraft becoming high on glide path while slowing to configure for landing. PF needed to use a sink rate higher than desired to return to glide slope. We met the published parameters at all of our approach gates, but the first portion of the approach was unstable. We landed safely on XXR and proceeded routinely to the gate.The main lesson learned was to slow earlier on final approach to allow a more stable approach. We accomplished all checklists and procedures and landed safely, but the crew would have been more able to look for potential threats if the PF had flown a more stable approach during the first portion of the approach. PNF was just back from several months off - take away for PNF was to address a rapidly evolving situation sooner and prompt the PF to configure sooner.
1761669: While on RNAV RWY 4 approach into UIN, between the initial fix (JISNA) and the FAF (WUSIS), we descended below the minimum altitude prescribed for that segment of the approach, which was 2100 ft. MSL . I did not recognize that we were below until about 1600 ft. MSL and by the time I had corrected our pitch and added power we between 1500 ft. and 1600 ft. MSL. We immediately climbed back up to 2100', and at about 2 miles prior to the FAF, we re-evaluated our position, flight guidance panel and configuration and felt that we could resume the approach as normal, which was an autopilot coupled LPV approach. Part of the cause of this issue was my set up of the flight guidance panel. We had been descending from about 7000 ft. and navigating direct to the initial fix of JISNA. At some point in the descent, ATC cleared us for the approach and told us to maintain 2700 ft. until JISNA. We were given the frequency change from Center to CTAF at this point as well. At that point, I thought I was in VNAV mode and descending. I hit APPR (Approach), since we were cleared for the approach, and dialed my altitude selector to the bottom of the approach, which was 960 ft. MSL for the minimums. My assumption was that we would then VNAV to 2700 ft. at JISNA, or essentially just VNAV to 2100 ft. by WUSIS, grab the glideslope and continue the descent. I felt I had set it up so that all stepdown altitudes would be met. At that point, I may have become distracted with other radio calls and prepping for landing. During this time, the SIC (Second In Command) was running checklists, trying to reach the FBO on unicom, and also conferring with ATC to ensure we had a good way to cancel IFR once we were on the ground. Neither of us were totally focused on the task at hand, which was to monitor the plane as we were beginning this approach. I estimate we were doing about an 800 fpm descent rate. We may have been in VNAV mode, but I was not coupled to the glide path, so we were descending in such a way that would not allow the autopilot to level us off at each fix. 1. PIC/SIC should have been totally focused on the primary task at hand: entering, establishing, and flying the approach as published. This would have caught any errors in my programming of the descent and flight guidance panel before we descended below published altitude. 2. Both pilots should be looking at the flight guidance panel in these critical times to verify proper mode, and calling out altitudes around these fixes. 3. Once the altitude deviation was realized, I should have climbed up, executed a missed approach, and called ATC to vector us back around for the approach. 4. My decision not to go missed was influenced by my desire to keep my passenger's schedule. That is a hazardous attitude that I want others to be aware of and learn from. As our passengers were boarding the plane, they decided to change the destination to UIN due to the fact we were unlikely to be able to get into ZZZ due to low ceilings. The altitude deviation occurred on the RNAV (Area Navigation) approach to RW 4 at UIN. We had been cleared for the approach and we were to instructed to maintain 2700 ft. until established on the approach and had been approved to change to advisory frequency. I was the nonflying pilot and was busy verifying everything on the checklist had been completed and communicating with KC center and UNICOM at UIN to make position reports. I also verified with KC center that we would be able to contact them on the ground using that frequency or did we need to cancel our IFR through flight service. This took a little extra time to complete due to my lack of experience with the Proline Fusion avionics so I was not monitoring the PFD as closely as I should have. We were inside JISNA (IAF)and I was trying to determine our position from the airport in order to give an accurate position report when the pilot flying said something to the effect of wait why are we low. He immediately added power selected vertical speed up and set our altitude selector to 2100 ft. I was focused on other tasks in the cockpit so I cannot say with 100% certainty what autopilot modes were selected previously. We were somewhere between 1600 ft. and 1500 ft. MSL when he started the recovery. We reached 2100 ft. two miles prior to the WUSIS (FAF) intercepted the glide path and landed without further issue. During the debrief with my captain after the flight we discussed the need to treat such a critical phase of flight with the utmost respect and after getting established on the approach to keep all attention on the task at hand which is flying/monitoring the approach. We also discussed the need to make a verbal call out of all autopilot/ flight director mode changes to make sure both pilots are on the same page and are totally aware of what the automation is doing if it is engaged.
1761674: We had just fully configured for landing, crossed the FAF and began our final descent on the RNAV RWY 17R approach into DWH. I was the pilot flying and had a customer pilot in the right seat for a demo flight. Tower called out traffic at our 1 o'clock and 2 miles unknown altitude that was apparently on final then began to turn north 'possibly NORDO'. We called visual and were instructed to continue the approach. Both of us in the cockpit saw Aircraft Y turning what looked to be base to final converging on our path. I broke off the final approach course to the left keeping Aircraft Y in sight and let tower know. Aircraft Y appeared to notice us as it made an abrupt climbing right turn away from us. Once I felt we had enough separation I elected to resume the approach, notified tower, received landing clearance and landed uneventfully. If I had to guess, we came within about 200-300 ft. of Aircraft Y. There is a lot of student traffic and flight schools at DWH. Aircraft Y was most likely a student training flight. Tower was transmitting in the blind to Aircraft Y repeatedly and told them not to circle on final and to look for light gun signals.Exercise heightened awareness when flying to/from airports where there is a lot of student training.
1761688: At 10,000 ft., sterile FD, descent into DFW, we began preparation procedures [in the] galley and cabin. Once finished, FA3 (Flight Attendant) asked who was in the forward lavatory and we determined the wheelchair passenger at 1F must have gone to the bathroom. FA3 knocked and told her we were landing now and to return to her seat now. She said, 'Ok, I'm coming.' FA1 & FA3 continued asking her to return to her seat and when the wheels dropped. She was still in the bathroom saying she was coming. FA3 and FA1 continued communicating with her and at less than 1 minute to landing the decision was made that she would not be able to safely make it to a seat and she was informed to 'stay in the lavatory.' The flight landed and taxied to toward Gate A19 at which time FA1 informed the Captain we had a passenger land in the lavatory. The Captain asked for basic information at this time. FA1 informed him that the passenger was still in the lavatory and if we were going to be stopped so she could return to her seat. The Captain stated, 'We're going to keep moving.' The passenger was told to remain in the lavatory until the seatbelt sign was turned off. Once we parked at the gate, the passenger came out on her own and apologized saying she was getting sick. FA1 confirmed her name as Passenger A. The Captain then brought FA1 into the cockpit and stated that he should have known we didn't have a passenger in their seat for landing and that he had to do reports now. After [the] Captain made [the] 'prepare for landing announcement' I, FA3 (Flight Attendant), walked up to [the] front and started clearing the cabin from there to [the] back. I finished preparing the cabin and headed up to my seat. When I was getting ready to sit, I saw that there was someone in front lavatory and asked FA1 if he saw anyone go in there. He explained that passenger 1F who came on [a] wheelchair had to use [the] lavatory last minute. I noticed how close we were getting to the ground so I started knocking on [the] door and told her, 'We are approaching landing and you need to come out;' to which she responded, 'I'm coming;' so I kept knocking on door and telling her she needed to come out already. Then, I noticed the landing gear is coming out. I then tell her, 'You need to come out NOW, landing gear is down we are about to land.' She said, 'Okay;' and seemed like she was going to come out but then didn't. That's when FA1 got up and told tell her to stay in the lavatory, which at that point, [was] so close to [the] ground and [since there was] such little time, [it] seemed like the best decision.We landed safely and checked on [the] passenger, she said she was okay. FA1 called [the] flight deck and explained to the Captain that we had someone in the lavatory [and] to let us know if we were going to make any stops so that we could have her go back to [her] seat safely since it takes her time to walk to her seat. The Captain told FA1, 'We are going to keep moving;' so [the] passenger remained in [the] lavatory until we came to a safe stop. The passenger came out and apologized for what she had done and said she understood she had done wrong but she really needed to go. Captain asked us why we didn't call him in the air we explained everything happened just so suddenly and we were so close to [the] ground with sterile flight deck and basically not much time.
1761698: I was told to go to the gate at ZZZ airport to inspect a write up on an ERJ175. The write up stated that the pilots were not able to get cool air in the cockpit during cruise, but the packs worked and blew cool air on ground. It was written up previously and was a repeat write up. Because this was a repeat and there were no EICAS (Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System) messages reported, I decided to interrogate the CMC (Central Maintenance Computer) for active faults and faults stored on the previous flight. I found two fault codes on the current leg as active with no inactive time stamp showing it was resolved. I then went to active faults and both codes were stored as active there as well. The two fault codes were 21000020AM2 and 21000030AM2. Following the FIM (Fault Isolation Manual), the problem was a fault with SPDA (Secondary Power Distribution Assembly) 2 Module 26. I inspected the MEL (Minimum Equipment List) list and there was no deferral for this item. I informed my lead and ordered parts needed for repair. The parts would not arrive until the next morning so I was told it would be days. Shortly after arriving at work, I was informed that it was signed off as left pack deferred and flew out. Looking at the fault codes, the fault was for more than just the pack system which made it non-deferrable.Days did not follow the turn over stating that the faults were active and that the problem was with the SPDA 2 Module 26. They also did not look up fault in FIM and followed the procedures. This allowed for a broken plane to have a different part to be deferred while the actual problem was not addressed. Mechanics need to follow manuals and carefully read shift turnover.
1761704: Aircraft X was operating on an IFR flight plan, and was transitioning through the practice area. The instructor onboard exhibited defiance and no acknowledgement of wrongdoing, exhibiting Macho, Invulnerability, and Anti-Authority. 1761720: We had a near mid-air collision with a fairly large drone operating between 3,200 and 3,500 feet MSL (2,000-2,300 feet AGL). My student spotted the drone out of his window, and after rolling the wings to view the drone, I confirmed the drone was well-within 500 feet of the aircraft. We circled the drone and reported it to Approach [Control], and continued our flight well south of the area the drone was spotted over. We recommend that operators are extremely vigilant to look out for drones while operating at all altitudes, even those where drone use is prohibited. 1761723: [Report narrative contained no additional information.] The crew and plane had arrived 4 hours earlier (XA:46) on an empty reposition leg. The passengers were originally scheduled to arrive at XC:00. The flight plan was delayed through handler 4 times due to uncertainty of passenger arrival time, with the most recent scheduled target takeoff time of XE:30.After engine start, the crew was instructed to taxi to Runway 05 holding point 'Hotel'. The aircraft initially stopped at H1 as a smaller business jet was taking Runway 05. We reported 'holding point H1' and the Controller responded 'holding point Hotel hold short Runway 05'. We moved forward the short distance from holding point Hotel 1 to Hotel. The Controller stated, 'Aircraft X, be prepared for an immediate takeoff. Do you have traffic 4 mile final in sight?' I responded 'affirmative, traffic in sight.' The Tower issued another instruction and I read back 'Line up and wait Runway 5, be ready for immediate takeoff.' We taxied ahead briefly then the Tower instructed us to 'hold position.' The Tower Controller stated that we were instructed 'Behind landing traffic, line up and wait Runway 5, be ready for immediate takeoff.' I replied that I heard 'Line up and wait Runway 5, be ready for immediate takeoff.'The Tower Controller was speaking with 2 inbound aircraft on the ILS (Instrument landing System) for Runway 5. There was another aircraft intercepting the ILS approximately 12 miles out. The inbound aircraft had been on a 4 mile final when we crossed the hold short point by approx. 100 ft. It was instructed to go around at approximately 2 miles out. After the inbound aircraft started its go-around, we were instructed to 'line up and wait, Runway 5.' We were cleared for takeoff and the Tower Controller stated that he would be submitting a report.A rough estimate indicates that the distance between holding point H and the actual runway is approximately 650 ft. We taxied about one 100 ft. across the hold short line but stopped approximately 500 ft. short of entering the runway. The term 'selective attention bias' seems appropriate here. I heard part of a message that included the phrase 'be ready for immediate takeoff' and was ready to act quickly. This situation was complicated by a language barrier and I missed or didn't understand the first part of the Controller's message of 'after landing traffic'. Operating frequently at busy Class B airports in the US where it's not unusual to be expected to expedite takeoff with closely spaced traffic, this situation was not out of the ordinary. In hindsight, it was the intention of the Controller to put us between the landing traffic and the next aircraft that was 12 miles out, not in front of the first aircraft that was landing.What both crew members could agree on is that we heard a transmission with an instruction to 'Line up and wait Runway 05. Be prepared for an immediate takeoff'.Contributing factors included language as LIEO is a popular international destination. There are many non-native English speakers on frequency. Phraseology can be different than what is used in the US and when accents and cultures are mixed, message transmission and reception aren't always in alignment.Time pressure [was a factor]. There had been numerous delays in the schedule. There was a sense of wanting to 'get things moving' since we were running 3 hours late. The weather at subsequent airports were forecast to have low ceilings and possible fog, so we didn't want to endure any unnecessary delays. The scheduled takeoff time of XE:30 was close to expiring.Also we were expecting to be sequenced into landing traffic and the pace was rapid. The instruction 'Be prepared for an immediate takeoff' had us ready to respond quickly. Recent landing experience [corroborated this]. Upon arrival 4 hours earlier, we were given landing clearance a few miles out. Instructions had a bit of a 'at the last minute' feel.PNF (Pilot Not Flying) had a Bose noise cancelling headset and PF(Pilot Flying) had a Telex over-the-ear headset. Neither pilot understood the first part of the ATC transmission. PF thought PNF might have understood the message better since he had a higher performance headset. What we did correctly [includes the following]. We read back what we thought we heard, assuming we would be corrected if wrong. We proceeded slowly across the hold short line. We stopped immediately when instructed and did not enter runway. We kept the incoming aircraft in sight and watched it go-around.What we did incorrectly [includes the following]. PNF missed or didn't understand the first part of an ATC transmission and didn't ask for clarification from the Controller or confirmation from the other pilot. With the 'Be prepared for immediate takeoff' instruction, we were spring-loaded to react versus stopping to ask for the message to be repeated or have a discussion between 2 pilots. [Also] since there was ambiguity in what we heard, we should have asked for clarification. After operating at busy class B airports in the US, there's a bit of hesitation in stopping to ask for an instruction to be repeated. Doing this at such an airport can result in getting lectured by ground and tower controllers.
1761724: I was doing some pattern work at my home field to work on my landings and maintain currency. After receiving permission to taxi to XXL behind a business jet, I confirmed with Tower that I was cleared for XXL. In hindsight, I may have missed a radio call from Tower, and similarly during Run Up I had to repeat my initial call to Ground.Once in the air I completed one circuit of the pattern without issue.On a subsequent circuit I was to land behind another aircraft ahead of me. I made my base turn, at which point Tower notified me that I was cutting off an aircraft behind me. I thought I was number 2 for XXR, but it turns out I was number 3. During this time, if I recall correctly, there was a change of staff in process at the Tower and I had to change frequency. I know I missed a call at this point.On the next circuit the controller called my crosswind turn after takeoff. Traffic appeared to be busy plus there was another aircraft in the vicinity that the controller mentioned was not responding to radio calls. I continued flying west, as I had silence on the radios, then received a call from Tower telling me that my next landing would be full stop. I complied with that.After landing on XXR I exited [the runway]. I was then directed to taxi and hold short of XXL. Upon stopping short of XXL the communications in my aircraft died. Surprising as the alt has been showing a positive charge. My medical has a restriction where I can't accept light gun signals during the daytime. As I was already on the ground there was no way I could divert, squawk 7600. Fortunately as a comms backup I have the tower's phone no. in my cell phone so I called the tower, explained where I was and that I had lost comms. I was directed to cross XXL and taxi straight into the ramp.I advised the front desk at the flight school/club about the radio issues and they said they would let the mechanic know.In future, if I think I am missing radio calls, I will try and confirm such with ATC ideally during the run up. Also, despite the METAR noting 10 SM visibility, the haze in the air from forest fires may have contributed to spotting other aircraft.
1761732: Flight was from ZZZ-ZZZ1 IFR clearance in VMC albeit some smoke.Flight was cleared to 14,000 feet then changed to 13,000 after passing 12,000. Looking directly into the sun through smoky haze I did not get it level at 13,000 and busted. ATC made no comment, perhaps due late change. No traffic in the area and no conflicts. 1761737: Apparently one of the flight school aircraft, a Cessna 172-L model, has been technically un-airworthy. The local mechanic shop did perform a pre-buy inspection when the flight school purchased the aircraft. The aircraft has undergone routine 100 hour inspections since the plane started working in the flight school. However, it wasn't until the most recent 100 hour inspection which was early September of this year that the local mechanic shop found that the aircraft was overdue on an Airworthiness Directive on a component on the propeller. It was overdue for about 500 hours on that particular AD. The mechanic shop was not certified to do the inspection on the propeller for that given AD for the propeller to be complied with. The flight school requested a ferry permit to fly the aircraft to the nearest propeller mechanic shop but was denied by the local FSDO. The next option was to remove the propeller and drive it to a propeller shop so that AD could be complied with. Such action was taken and the propeller shop found no defects with the propeller. The propeller was later driven back to the home airport to be placed back on the aircraft. Alas, the aircraft was complied with all known Airworthiness directives. The local mechanic shop staff admitted that they overlooked the AD. However, at the end of the day it is the owner/operator of the aircraft that is ultimately responsible for determining the airworthiness of the aircraft, which includes me, the flight instructor when using the aircraft to train student pilots. The flight school staff, meaning all the instructors and chief pilot were essentially responsible for this oversight of the airworthiness of the aircraft. I believe that the flight school staff trusted the mechanic shop to ensure the aircraft complies with all known AD's for every 100 hour inspection. The flight school has every intention to ensure the aircraft meets all inspections including ADs, and that by paying the mechanic shop for their services would suffice for ensuring the aircraft is airworthy. Over-relying on the mechanic shop in my opinion has been the root cause of this issue. I've personally shown the logbooks of the aircraft and ADs to my students prior to every checkride to show the aircraft is airworthy. I've even presented the ADs to my examiner for my CFI initial checkride. I honestly just never knew how to look up ADs or even know how to make sure that all ADs are complied with. The resolution that the chief pilot and I want to take to prevent this mishap from happening again is to learn how to look up ADs ourselves as a secondary check on top of the routine inspections done by the mechanics. Had I known that the AD wasn't complied with no one would've flown that aircraft until it is absolutely airworthy. A more thorough overview on the flight school's ADs is needed to make sure we are complying with them, and to make sure none have been overlooked. Again, the Chief pilot and I want to be able to double check AD compliance after routine inspections, and enhance communication between the instructors and mechanics.
1761740: While practicing landings in the pattern at ZZZ. Myself and my student were downwind at 1400 feet MSL when we noticed a drone flying at the same altitude but heading north directly in our path. This drone seemed to resemble that of an amateur photography style not a professional.
1761743: I was flying the RNAV (GPS) 34 straight in approach into FHR. The airport wall veiled in smoke/haze. The approach went well and I had visual contact with the airport 2 miles out. As I approached the runway, I was a little high and floated, so I decided to go-around. It was a mental slip. As I was flying downwind, I realized that I messed up, but I had visual contact with the airport and at that point thought it was safer to continue the pattern. I turned to base and then as I turned to final, I turned late. I decided then that I would just over fly the airport and fly the published missed. I contacted Whitney Approach for instructions to get back on the approach. Approach rightfully rebuked me for the go-around and then gave me instructions to return me to the approach. I flew the approach and landed without incident. Key learning from this event:1. If you cannot land for any reason, you must fly the published missed, regardless of prevailing conditions, unless you have cancelled IFR with ATC or until ATC has given other instructions.2. As time permits, scan the missed procedure on final to aid in preparation.3. Increase the time spent briefing the missed procedure when briefing the approach.
1761748: Aircraft X was in my Tower pattern, making right traffic for Runway 17R. Aircraft Y was given left downwind for Runway 17R. I told Aircraft Y change to Runway 17L, Runway 17L clear to land, and he read it back. Aircraft X was on a 2-mile final when Aircraft Y turned base. I gave Aircraft Y, traffic 2-mile final, Aircraft X, for the parallel runway. Aircraft Y said, I thought I was cleared to Runway 17R. I said negative, Runway 17L cleared to land. At the time Aircraft X took evasive maneuvers. Aircraft Y landed on the right and Aircraft X said we are on the go with that near miss. Aircraft Y was given possible pilot deviation. 1761764: On approach into ZZZ on ILS XR we had been asked to keep our speed up until the marker. We complied with the request. The weather was very gusty winds and both myself and the pilot flying communicated as to what the V-ref target speeds should be. Sometime before 1000 feet the pilot flying was trying to control his speed and configure at the last minute in order to comply with the Tower's request. We had traffic about 3 1/2 miles in front of us. With the gusty winds and both of us pilots being relatively new to the aircraft and because this aircraft was an X type aircraft I had relayed to the pilot flying that we didn't want to have a tail strike with such gusty winds, so I suggested that at any time either one of us felt that we weren't going to land in the touchdown zone or we didn't feel we weren't going to make a normal landing then we needed to 'go-around.' About 1200 feet we got another gusty wind report from the Tower that caused me to readjust the target speed with my head being down and losing situational awareness (SA). We never got too fast for our configuration but I called the'1000 feet' call at approximately 930 feet. I had already configured the aircraft for the landing checklist except for final flaps. I feel the pilot flying got distracted by me changing the target speeds that he lost his SA and forgot to call for flaps 30/landing checklist. I initiated the checklist and realized we were hadn't gone to flaps 30 and he hadn't called for the checklist. I selected final flaps and finished the checklist. I called 500 feet and he responded stable and we landed uneventfully. On arrival into ZZZ I was configured flaps 15, 180 knots until the marker. About the time I was going to call flaps 30 we received a new gusting wind report from tower that required an adjustment to our target speed. We discussed the wind and adjusted for about a 15 knot add over flaps 30 ref of about 148 target speed. Upon completing landing checklist which at this point was also delayed and we discovered that the flaps were not positioned yet to 30. We immediately positioned the flaps to 30 and landed. The flaps 15 speed I was flying was very close to the new target speed and the aircraft was stable with respect to airspeed altitude and course. Contributing factors can include my new position as a requalification on the aircraft with only about 4 landings this year.
1761771: All pilot crew members were present at scheduled report time, and pre-flight planning was accomplished as a crew. We arrived at the aircraft together approximately one hour before scheduled push time. Flight deck preparation duties were accomplished uneventfully in accordance with SOP. During flight deck preparation, I was designated by the Captain as the Pilot Monitoring for the first leg. The Captain accomplished the departure briefing, and I do not recall any deviations from the standard briefing. We pushed one minute early and proceeded uneventfully to Runway XXC. There were no aircraft anomalies during start and taxi. When cleared by ATC and after accomplishing runway verification, we initiated the takeoff roll. Another heavy aircraft had just departed on the same runway. The Captain made the 'check thrust' callout, and I replied with the 'thrust set' callout. After verifying all three airspeed indicators were matched and increasing, I focused my attention on the engine instruments while periodically cross-checking the airspeed indicator. All aircraft systems appeared to be performing normally, and I noticed normal aircraft acceleration. I glanced down the runway once prior to making the '100 knots' callout to verify that we were tracking centerline, then remained inside the cockpit until the Captain initiated the reject. I don't recall any significant yaw during the takeoff roll other than normal motion associated with the tracking of runway centerline. Approaching V1 (Takeoff Decision Speed), the Captain pulled the throttles to idle, initiating a rejected takeoff. I was surprised by this action, as I had not sensed a condition requiring a rejected takeoff. I did not hear a 'reject' callout. I noticed the speedbrake handle deploy and felt the RTO (Rejected Takeoff) brakes engage, but I do not remember looking to verify that the thrust reversers were in reverse. I heard the 'V1' callout shortly after the reject was initiated. I did not make the '80 knots' callout. When we were almost stopped, I made a 'remain seated, remain seated' PA announcement. I reported to ATC that we had rejected on runway XXC and that we were stopped on the runway between the five and six boards. I was confused about why the Captain had rejected the takeoff. I assumed he had seen something that I hadn't, and I was searching the instrument panel for the reason. The Captain said he felt a pronounced right swerve that felt like an engine failure, which prompted him to reject the takeoff. The IRO suggested looking at the wheels synoptic to check for a blown tire, but there was no indication of one. At the IRO's recommendation, we completed the rejected takeoff non-normal checklist. We did not request emergency vehicle response. We taxied clear of the runway and held position for a few minutes with the parking brake released while monitoring brake temperatures. I recall the hottest brake being number 7 with a value of 7.7. With brake temperatures no longer increasing, we elected to taxi to the gate, and coordinated with ATC, Operations and [Maintenance Control] for a gate return. We accomplished the BRAKE TEMP non-normal during the taxi back to the gate. Upon blocking in, we debriefed Maintenance in the cockpit and then departed the aircraft with the parking brake released after accomplishing all post-flight duties and a flight crew debrief. I spoke with [Operations] and completed a human factors questionnaire with her. While accomplishing flight deck preparation after plane swap and re-release, I was released from the trip.I recall V1 being 137 knots. I estimate the reject was initiated at approximately 130 knots, because I heard the automated 'V1' callout occur just after the reject was initiated. The 'V1' callout definitely occurred after the reject was initiated, because I remember being confused by sensing the deceleration at the same time as hearing the 'V1' callout. I suspect there was some residual acceleration after the throttles were pulled to idle which triggered the 'V1' callout, but by the time I heard the callout we were already decelerating. I was in the Jumpseat. It was the Captains takeoff runway XXC. At 120 to 130 knots, the Captain rejected the takeoff without announcing the Reject.The airplane came to a complete stop on the runway. A few seconds passed, I said, who's gonna say remain seated? The FO (First Officer) said, I will, and made the remain seated call over the PA.I said, we need to tell ATC we rejected. The FO then let ATC know.I realize that the ATC call comes before the remain seated call. My biggest concern at that moment was the possibility of an un-commanded passenger evacuation. And since no one in the cockpit was saying or doing anything yet, I strongly suggested that someone say, REMAIN SEATED.A few seconds went by. I said, should we do the Rejected takeoff checklist? The CA (Captain) agreed and called for it.The FO began to read the checklist, then the Cabin call message displayed. I asked the Captain, do you want me to get that? He said yes.The FA (Flight Attendant) on the phone asked if things were ok, then asked if we were going to make an announcement. I asked the Captain if he wanted to make a PA, he directed me to make an announcement. I said, ladies and gentlemen, we have rejected the takeoff due to an abnormality, we are running a checklist, please remain seated with your seatbelts fastened and follow your flight attendants instructions. As I finished the announcement, the FO was on step 5 of the rejected takeoff checklist.The CA announced that he wanted to taxi clear of the runway and he released the brakes. I said, should we make sure that the tires are ok first? The FO selected the gear synoptic page. All tire pressures were normal, but brake temperatures were 3.5 and rising. The FO then continued with the Rejected takeoff Checklist.I began to smell hot brakes in the cockpit, a hot rubber smell. Just then the cabin call light illuminated, I answered and the FA said that there was a hot rubber smell near door 3. I told her it was the brakes and that we would make an announcement. The Captain then directed me to make another announcement.I said, ladies and gentleman, what you are smelling is the elevated temperature of the brakes, the indications are within limits, please remain seated and follow the flight attendants instructions while we finish our checklists. The FO asked if we should call the fire trucks. The Captain said no I think we're ok.Tower then asked us what the reason was for the rejected takeoff. The Captain told the FO that the airplane had an un-commanded yaw to the right. The FO relayed that information to Tower.As we taxied clear of the runway the Captain said that he felt a yaw and thought that an engine had failed, that's why he rejected.The Captain said let's go back to the gate, and directed the FO to call [Operations]. I interjected and said do you think we should call maintenance first? He said yes.I called maintenance, explained the situation, I gave them the brake temps and asked their opinion on returning to the gate. Local maintenance said it would be fine to go to the gate. In hind sight, I should have called [Maintenance Control], but at the time it was more efficient to call local maintenance on the radio.As we taxied to the gate I asked the Captain not to pull into the gate until I reviewed the rejected takeoff, and performance sections of the FM (Flight Manual). Even though I just asked maintenance, I wanted to be sure there were no restrictions on bringing an airplane with hot brakes to the gate.I pulled up and reviewed [the FM sections] with the CA and FO. A BRAKE TEMP advisory message was now displayed.We parked the airplane at the gate and maintenance came to the cockpit. One of the mechanics had a laptop. He asked the Captain what happened and typed the Captains response into his laptop. The Captain said he felt a severe yaw to the right, he thought it was an engine failure and he rejected the takeoff. [Maintenance] asked the FO if he felt the yaw, the FO said, not really. [Maintenance] asked me if I felt the yaw, I told him that I felt a yaw to the left after the CA began the rejected takeoff maneuver.[Maintenance] then said that he downloaded the data from the airplane and that no anomalies were found. The Captain said then maybe it was a gust of wind that yawed the airplane to the right. I told [Maintenance] that the Quick Turnaround Landing Weight Limit was not exceeded and I referenced the FM performance section with him. In hind sight, I should have advised the CA and FO to include the information outlined in FO in their rejected takeoff maintenance write up.The mechanics left, the Captain then debriefed. He said that he felt a significant yaw to the right, he said that he did not announce 'REJECT' and that he should have. He thanked us for backing him up.We went to the new airplane. I did the exterior preflight. I got a call from the [Flight Ops Manager] who asked me a list of HF (Human Factors) questions to gauge my stress level. I answered her questions.15 minutes later the Captain's phone rang, it was the chief pilot who advised us that a safety investigation is underway on the event and that we were being pulled off line with pay.
1761773: I made a delayed turn from base to final approach while conducting the ILS XXR into ZZZ. The reason for the delayed turn was a momentary lapse in CRM skills. I was the flying pilot, my copilot was the monitoring pilot. We were on a base leg when the Controller gave us a turn towards the final approach. I remember dialing in the correct heading, but forgot to press heading select. About ten seconds or so elapsed before the Controller asked if we were turning. I realized my error and immediately pressed heading select. The Controller gave us a new heading and an approach clearance. We turned onto final with a slight overshoot and above the glide slope. We configured for landing and used vertical speed mode to intercept the glide slope from above. We were on speed and altitude well before the 1,500 foot gate. Other than the late turn and the high glide slope intercept, there was no other incident or error.The fact is the I/we made an error by not following through with Verbalize Verify and Monitor. I know that we both verbalized the heading change, I recall we both Verified setting the heading, we both, however, forgot to monitor the FMAs for the change. I think that we realized the something wasn't right a split second before the controller queried us. There were many threats preceding this error. This is an all-night flight with an early morning low visibility arrival. The airspace is quite congested and there were many aircraft with similar sounding call signs. We had a runway change while on the arrival and the Controller kept us little higher and gave us a turn a little earlier than we had expected. I had a scheduling change in the middle of this pairing which reduced my rest time a day before this leg. Do to the current global pandemic and the reduced airline schedules, neither of us had flown very much in the past six months. I know I felt a bit rusty and tired.To mitigate this I gave what I thought was a good approach brief before top of descent, and we briefed the changed approach during the arrival. We still failed to monitor the FMA change at a crucial moment. It was an error I hope I/we don't repeat.
1761776: Upon climb out from runway 28R in ORD the Captain was unable to trim the stabilizer nose up with the yoke electric trim switch. He advised me of this and I helped him with manual trim from the trim wheel. We leveled off at 5,000 ft. and 250 knots for controllability and received permission from ATC to fly a box pattern to troubleshoot. We subsequently slowed to 230 knots for the pattern.We accomplished the Electronic Stabilizer Trim Inoperative procedure and got a patch through to [Maintenance Control] with dispatch monitoring on radio. Maintenance agreed with the procedure and with our decision to return to ORD. A flaps 15 landing was safely performed per the checklist and the aircraft was returned to [the] Gate.
1761777: I was conducting an initial Operating Experience with a First Officer (FO) who is new to the aircraft. As we started our takeoff roll the Flight Deck door swung open. A Flight Attendant immediately closed the door and it was indicating locked. I was positive I checked the Flight Deck door 'OPEN' light during the After Start Checklist and it was out. I believe the door became unlocked during an electrical power transfer issue caused by me.When I called for the After Start Checklist, I was momentarily distracted while watching the FO perform his flows. I neglected to turn on the engine generators at the beginning of the flow. When the FO turned off the APU, we momentarily lost power (I immediately caught the mistake right when he was turning off the APU). I believe this may have electrically unlocked the door.Contributing factors: Not much sleep the night before.This was our first flight together.I flew 2 days last week after not flying for 6 months.It was right at dawn and I had the lights on dim just as the sun was starting to shine into the cockpit. I may have seen the blue Generator OFF BUS lights if the switch was on bright.
1761811: While we were instructed to join the Runway XXC localizer ZZZ, Approach Controller handed us over to Tower Frequency. As soon as we joined the localizer, flying conditions started to deteriorate and became turbulent. Airspeed was fluctuating at 1,400 feet AGL. As a result of this, I had started to get focused on stable approach criteria, and work load gradually increased for both pilots. Over emphasis on stable approach criteria caused a distraction and both PF and PM forgot to obtain the landing clearance. Aircraft landed without any further incidents exited the runway and hold short of XXL. Since we did not hear anything from the Tower, both pilots became aware of the event and switched to Tower Frequency. Flight was completed without further incidents.Tunnel vision on stable approach parameters and Airspeed variations caused distraction. Since COVID-19 breakout, I was not flying as frequently as before. I believe this was factored into this incident.Give some extra time to double check all the required tasks are completed. As we are not flying as frequently as before, configure the aircraft early and passing 500 feet AGL, both pilots verbally verify one last time 'Cleared to Land.'
1761831: This flight was planned on a route that went through ZZZZ. In my pre-flight planning process, I checked the enroute NOTAMs by loading all the enroute FIR boundaries and then using 'control-F' and searching the enroute NOTAMs for applicable airways. Today, there were no such hits when performing this NOTAM checking method. Unfortunately, there was a NOTAM for ZZZZ that had been issued just before I arrived for work:...DUE TO COVID-19...ATS WILL NOT BE AVAILABLE. ATS CONTINGENCY PLAN(AIC A11/18) FOR ZZZZ1 FIR ACT. The flight had been airborne for some time, but was still in ZZZZ2 airspace when the crew advised me that they were being re-routed out of ZZZZ airspace - the re-route was minimal and after considerable effort (due to non-existent or out-of-date info in AIR for ZZZZ and ZZZZ3) I was finally able to speak with ZZZZ3 ATC and obtain an expected route through their airspace, and then I was able to advise the crew of the routing. The amount of en-route FIR boundary NOTAMs is daunting - impossible to read these for every international flight --- therefore using the 'Control-F' to search for applicable airways allows the Dispatcher to quickly determine if there are any en-route implications to the flight. Of course, if there are no associated airways with a NOTAM as in the case of the situation affecting this flight, then pertinent closures can be missed. In addition, since the crews do not receive a copy of the FIR boundary NOTAMs, this scenario leaves the Dispatcher as the single point of failure.Be smarter when it comes to FIR boundary NOTAMs. Utilize a resource like 'SmartNotam' to weed through all the FIR boundary NOTAMs and then provide both the crew and the dispatcher a condensed list of applicable FIR boundary NOTAMs to read and decipher.
1761842: I was the First Officer and PF ZZZ1-ZZZ. This was my first flight after not flying for over two months. The majority of the flight went fine, but as we approached ZZZ, ATC left us high (11,000 feet) very close to the airport. I was about to ask for lower when ATC gave us a descent. I thought we had just enough time to successfully descend and slow down, but when we were around 4,000 feet, ATC gave us a turn that made it clear they were directing us straight to the FAF. This was not what I was expecting, and left us high and fast and greatly increased our workload. I used the flight spoilers to slow down and then forgot to stow them after slowing enough to add flaps. Our workload was still quite high at this point, so we didn't realize the flight spoilers were still deployed until the spoiler caution message at 500 feet. At this point, the Captain immediately stowed them and we continued the landing.Because ATC left us high and then turned us directly to the FAF, our workload greatly increased. I deployed the spoilers in order to slow down, and then forgot to stow them because I was distracted by other things in the flight deck (arming the approach, making sure we intercepted the localizer and glideslope, making sure we were on speed and deployed our flaps and gear at the appropriate time, etc.). I was expecting something different from ATC and had a good plan in my head, but was thrown off when ATC gave us something I didn't expect. This was also my first leg after not flying for over 2 months, which I think could have contributed as well, because I was a bit rusty and a little bit slower than I normally am in the flight deck.We could have easily prevented this from happening by asking ATC for a longer downwind. I was planning a longer downwind in my head and when ATC gave us a turn directly to the FAF, we should have asked to stay on downwind instead. There wasn't anyone else out there to cause traffic issues, and it would have given us extra time to slow down and descend so that we weren't rushed. In the heat of the moment, I didn't think of this (though I used to remind my students of this option all the time when I was a flight instructor!), but I should have. When we stowed the spoilers, I decreased thrust and pitched down a little bit, which kept us on speed and caused only a slight deviation from the glideslope, which I was able to correct. Because of this, we made a completely normal landing. However, a go-around would also have been a good choice here, especially if we became unstable after retracting the spoilers.
1761844: On short final below 500 ft. the FO (First Officer) was flying and had an un-commanded stabilizer trim down. He stopped it with using the electric trim in the opposite direction correcting the out of trim condition and landed uneventfully. After landing we debriefed what happened and decided to write the malfunction up in the aircraft log. I was unaware that the FO was experiencing a problem with the trim until after landing.
1761850: I continued to land after still stabilizing an unstable visual approach below 500 feet AGL.Causes - Complacency, poor descent planning, minimal currency (I haven't been flying much recently).Lesson - Use multiple descent planning tools and techniques to improve vertical situational awareness and solidity feedback from other pilot on an approach.
1761883: I was conducting flight training with an instructor at ZZZ. The Bell 407 I was operating experienced contact between the main rotor and tail rotor drive shaft. The drive shaft was sheared after the helicopter was on the ground. The tower was notified and the aircraft was subsequently towed to hanger. While conducting autorotation training in a Bell-407 helicopter at ZZZ, I experienced a main rotor contact with the tail rotor driveshaft. The tail drive shaft sheared while on the ground at low rotor RPM. No injuries were sustained. Tower was notified and the helicopter was towed to a hangar. The FAA examined the helicopter, and the crew are scheduled to speak with the FAA.
1761885: I pre-flighted Aircraft X in ZZZ (departure airport) and noticed the trim wheel full forward during pre-flight. Took off in VMC/VFR to ZZZ1. The plane was sporting a brand new install GFC 500 autopilot. We used the autopilot on the way to ZZZ1. We climbed up to 9,500. It was bumpy as we approached the terrain around ZZZ1 so we slowed down considerably and descended for a landing. I was with my CFI friend who is a jet captain.Our flight club Treasurer called me and text me while in ZZZ1 after we had some breakfast. He said if you can please fly straight home as there may be an issue with the pitch trim and you should pull the autopilot circuit breaker. I asked him why he didn't mention that to me after he flew it the night before and when he noticed the problem then and he said he forgot. Asked why he didn't mention it to me in the morning before we left and he said we left early and he slept in. It's possible he didn't realize the severity of the problem. Perhaps he was flying a lot slower the previous night on descent and didn't face the same issue as us that day. Perhaps he didn't experience or realize the severity of the issue altogether.Before we left ZZZ1 we briefed the departure and planed on flying back to ZZZ via the desert. We also determined that not only should we pull the autopilot breaker but more importantly the pitch trim servo breaker. When we left ZZZ1 we departed runway 8 and climbed toward the NE. After clearing the terrain we turned west and settled in at cruise. My friend in the right seat was talking to a friend that was working Center. I decided to descend soon after we turned west to 6500 in a cruise descent. Listening to him talk to Center I didn't realize that after over a few minutes I had been pitching forward much more than normal. I noticed finally when the pitch trim was full forward to the stop and I was putting a lot of pressure on the control yoke to get the plane to descend on top of that. My friend asked for the flight controls and he almost immediately said I think we have a bound up flight cable and asked me if I agree we should make an emergency landing in ZZZ2 which was the closest airport. We slowed down (to go down) and that worked good enough thankfully. The trim wheel never moved back after that point even as we slowed and continued to descend. The control wheel full forward just made pushing on the control wheel forward a little easier. We landed and secured the plane and had a friend that lived [close] pick us up and take us back to ZZZ. We called our flight club leadership and told them the plane was down and something very serious was wrong with the flight controls.As we arrived to our cars at ZZZ almost four plus hours later we found three of the club board members (safety officer, maintenance officer and the treasurer) taking off in another club plane (C182). An hour later we curiously looked at the track log for that plane and sure enough they went from ZZZ to ZZZ2. Within 30 minutes or less of wheels down in the C182 the PA32 was on it's way back to ZZZ. They completely ignored that we downed the plane and almost certainly had no A&P look at the plane. I am writing this because the pattern just repeated with another member who had a redline oil temp in our club C172 and downed the plane in ZZZ3 and the exact same thing was done - they dismissed her account of the plane issue and flew it right back to base (ZZZ). She also had a CFI on board. The C172 has been having engine trouble for many months now and the club and maintenance shop can't figure out what's wrong with it. This was the latest episode of that ongoing issue.In my case when Aircraft X was returned to base it was down for nine days. The Treasurer who often doubles as a maintenance officer, wrote - 'The Aircraft X autopilot install highlighted an old nagging issue where the trim wheel was sometimes unable to achieve full down trim. The cables were replaced and the function is now fullyrestored.' The autopilot was installed maybe a week or two before this event. To this day I cannot get the club board to produce any ferry permit for the plane being returned to base, an A&P signing off on the plane before they returned it to base that day nor will they provide the aircraft maintenance logbook so we can see exactly what 'cables replaced' means immediately following our incident.I am writing this because a few members recently suggested it. I didn't realize that maybe I should have written this a little sooner following the event. I also learned that I may need to file [another] form because I experienced flight control issues in an aircraft. I will follow up on that as well hoping to be doing what is expected of me as a licensed pilot.
1761906: I was on LC1 with multiple aircraft in the south patter when Aircraft X checked in from the west requesting left traffic for runway 28L. LC2 was working runway 28R and the north pattern. I sequenced the pilot to follow Aircraft A on base turning final and also told the pilot about Aircraft Y on final for the parallel runway. Aircraft X reported the Cessna to follow in sight, so I cleared him to land. Aircraft X turned too early and I informed him that spacing between him and the Cessna was not going to work out. The pilot then says he's going to make a 360 and took action without realizing there is other traffic in his vicinity. I quickly informed him of traffic and he responded that he had traffic in sight. He made a right turn directly towards Aircraft Y who was on final for the parallel runway. Aircraft Y had to take evasive action to avoid Aircraft X. I told Aircraft X to go around and offset right of the runway and told him about traffic in the north pattern. He reported a Cessna in sight and began a turn to the right downwind quickly overtaking the Cessna on downwind. I instructed Aircraft X to extend downwind to follow traffic on final. He reported the Cessna to follow in sight (Aircraft B). Again, he turned base too early and I had to send the Cessna around to get Aircraft X to land.The pilot of Aircraft X may have misjudged the spacing required to follow aircraft that are much slower than a BE20. The pilot took action on his own without being aware of his surroundings. He should have verified with ATC before making any turns. As Aircraft X approached the MYF D airspace, crew noted there were approx 10 TCAS contacts within the D airspace. Crew discussed flying slow as possible to help see/avoid. Aircraft X was cleared into MYF class D by tower. We were cleared to join left downwind for Runway 28 Left. Just prior to downwind we lowered gear and flaps to fly as slow as possible (approx 120K IAS). Approaching abeam landing point tower told us to extend downwind and to take interval on an aircraft already on final to 28 Left. Flying Pilot saw aircraft on final and turned to take interval. We were also told there was an aircraft on long final to 28 Right. After turning to take interval on 28 Left traffic, Tower called and said something that made pilot flying think he was taking interval on the wrong aircraft...that there was another aircraft on final to 28 left. Pilot rolled toward level to look for other traffic. Doing so put us close to runway 28 Right final course. Pilot called tower and began to execute a right 180 to clear the final for both parallel runways. In the turn, pilot saw the aircraft that was making approach to Runway 28 Right and executed a level nose down maneuver to allow aircraft to fly over and laterally to the right. Tower told us the 28 Right aircraft flew over us. Aircraft X landed 28 Left and was told to contact tower for possible pilot deviation.Lesson learned. Tower told Aircraft X that he was flying 'fast' making sequence difficult with GA aircraft and that 28R is preferred runway for Aircraft X size/speed aircraft. Aircraft X reported that we requested 28L ONLY because we thought it would be easier for ATC not the crew. Given the traffic saturation it seemed a direct entry to left downwind to 28L would be preferable than overflying field to entering right downwind for 28R.Aircraft X reported to tower that they were flying as slow as possible and that if tower had preference to which runway they could have communicated that to Aircraft X. Also, tower informed Aircraft X that the two parallel runways use different control tower frequencies. Aircraft X did not have as good of SA on runway 28R since they couldn't hear the transmissions to/from that aircraft. ForeFlight EFB is used by the Aircraft X company pilots. ForeFlight lists both tower freqs but list one as 'secondary' not as for other runway. MYF AFD also does not say that there are different tower frequencies with one being for 28L and the other for 28R.Tower is probably hesitant to 'counter' which of the parallel runways the pilot has requested to land. However when a non-local aircraft if flying into an unfamiliar airport which is congested with many different types of aircraft. It would be helpful if Tower would make suggestions for appropriate runways. Pilot would still have prerogatives to stay with what was requested. AFD should have notes that indicate two different frequencies are used SIMULTANEOUSLY for the airport.See and avoid is still critical in VMC conditions. Just because Tower or Approach gives an aircraft a clearance to land...or vector if IFR the pilot still need to keep a look out to avoid collisions.
1761923: Descending into LGB on the DSNEE arrival, we were cleared to descend via the arrival. Captain was Pilot Flying. First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. ATC cleared us to descend via the arrival for Runway 30 but didn't specify which approach to expect. ATIS stated runway in use but not approach type. Captain loaded and briefed the RNAV (Z). While descending via, and inside the branch point for the arrival, Approach Control cleared us for the ILS via the arrival. At that time we were in VNAV/LNAV with the lowest altitude on the arrival set in the MCP. Our position was a few miles East of MCKYE and descending.Upon receiving the clearance the Captain quickly loaded the ILS and executed it without verifying there were no resultant discontinuities. Because we were inside the branch point of the arrival a discontinuity did appear, even though we were going to the same runway. Once the execute (EXEC) button was pushed the discontinuity appeared and VNAV disconnected. Because we were descending at the time, we continued to descend. The crossing restriction at MCKYE was at or above 7200'. The aircraft descended to roughly 6800' before the Captain corrected and returned us to the correct altitude. We were back up to 7200' prior to MCKYE. After correcting the flight path, the correct approach was loaded in the FMC and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.Proper verification prior to execution would help prevent this type of event from occurring again. Make sure both Crew Members have seen the changes and agree on them before pushing EXEC. Also, once the arrival has commenced do not execute any FMC changes unless you are on the LEGS page and have cleared any discontinuities resulting from the approach or runway change. We were on the DSNEE 4 Arrival for LGB and had previously entered the RNAV Y MIDDS transition (I did not close the MIDDS discontinuity per SOP). Weather was IMC due to fires in Southern California. We had been cleared to descend via and 4000' MSL was entered in the MCP window with VNAV PATH. Approximately 1 NM prior to DSNEE waypoint, we were given clearance for the ILS to Runway 30. I re-entered the arrival with the MIDDS transition for the ILS and immediately got a VNAV discontinuity from the FMC due to the re-entry. We were working on closing the discontinuity when I noticed the aircraft had descended 400' below the MCKYE restriction of 7200' MSL, approximately 3 NM prior to MCKYE. I immediately initiated a climb back to 7200' MSL to MCKYE and continued the descend via arrival. We did not see any traffic conflicts from TCAS and ATC did not mention anything.Expect the unexpected. I should have entered the next restriction altitude in the MCP before making changes to the arrival. Even though I did not expect a discontinuity, it would have been prudent because we were on the arrival and close to a fix with a restriction. Surprise at the discontinuity delayed action. I should have concentrated more on the restrictions and less on the FMC.
1761932: On a climb to FL230 Denver center called traffic at FL240 converging. We were in marginal VFR due to smoke and did not have the traffic in sight until he was flying over us. The autopilot and autothrottle were engaged in VNAV and the aircraft was leveling at FL230 when we received a reduce vertical speed RA at FL227. I disconnected all automation and leveled the airplane at FL228 per RA pitch commands on the Primary Flight Display. The TCAS showed the other aircraft 1,100 feet above us at that point. When the traffic cleared. I climbed to FL230 and we reported the incident to ATC.
1761944: While conducting a leg from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on day two of a four-day, we had just climbed to cruise altitude, FL390, and leveled off. I, [the] CA (Captain), was Pilot Flying and we got a CARGO BTL LO caution on the EICAS. I said that I had the radios and controls and asked the non-flying FO (First Officer) to reference the QRH for the CARGO BTL LO indication. He read the checklist carefully, FIRE page 16, and it called for AFT CARGO switch off and then land at the nearest suitable airport. We switched the AFT CARGO switch to the OFF position. While reading the checklist, the CARGO BTL LO caution message disappeared from EICAS. We completed the checklist.I asked the FO to take the radios and contacted Dispatch by ACARS. I told them that we had had the CARGO BTL LO indication, and while conducting the checklist, the indication went away. We completed the checklist and the next action would be to divert to the nearest suitable field. Through ACARS, I asked for weather at several potential divert locations. ACARS response was to ask if we still had the indication, and we responded again that we did not. The Dispatcher then stated that he didn't think that we had to divert... I messaged that a divert was called for by the checklist and [that we] needed recommendations on where to go immediately. While having this conversation through ACARS, I was having a conversation with the FO about the problem and talking with ATC about the potential divert. Since the information on weather was not available from Dispatch, I asked ATC for weather at several potential alternates. While giving us the weather, they asked if [we] were declaring an emergency. We stated NO, that we were working the problem and negotiating with our Dispatch... The FO and I discussed the problem. While reading the checklist, The CARGO BTL LO indication went away. The checklist, Fire page 16, was not clear and did not state any reference to, if the indication went away - divert or just continue. We discussed the actions called for by the checklist- AFT CARGO SWITCH - OFF. Turning off the AFT CARGO switch would close the value isolating the Aft Cargo Container from the cabin and would have no connection with the CARGO BTL LO indication. We had no indication that the bottle had been discharged... but it could simply leak. The divert would be called for because without redundant fire bottles, we would have reduced fire protection in the Aft Cargo area. I voiced my concern that, possibly, a divert was not called for in this case - but maybe it was... I was thinking it through....By that time, Dispatch was responding that we should NOT divert. That they had contacted Maintenance and Maintenance said that a divert was not necessary in this case. I responded with - THANKS, but I would like that response in writing from the CHIEF PILOT. As CA, I had decided that it was probably ok to continue, but since a divert was called for by the checklist I would need to do it as a precaution. Since Dispatch and Maintenance thought that it was NOT necessary, I wanted a second opinion on not complying with the checklist, and having it come from a seasoned Chief Pilot seemed like a good idea. As we were having these lengthy series of texts through ACARs, we planned our possible divert. As we were nearing our decision point - we had selected ZZZ2 as our divert airport - we received an ACARS from the Dispatch that the CHIEF PILOT concurred, that a divert was not necessary. OK, we responded. We are continuing on to our destination we messaged. We continued and landed at our destination with no issues. On the walk around, the FO checked the AFT CARGO BTLs. They were full.As the Captain, I had to make a decision to divert or continue while following the checklist, company policy, asking for inputs from FO, [the] Company, Maintenance etc., and using my own brain and experience. No checklist or Dispatch, or even Chief Pilot recommendations could absolve me of that responsibilityI chose to continue the flight to our destination rather than divert as called for by the checklist because the CARGO BTL LO indication went away, while taking on the inputs from Dispatch, Maintenance and the agreement of the Chief Pilot. But maybe I made the wrong choice?? We landed safely and now can look back and try to learn from the experience.We need real time weather information available in the cockpit. While we had plenty of time - [it was a] land as soon as SUITABLE emergency - it was still an emergency and we were unable to get weather information from Dispatch in a timely manner. I suggest a clarification in the checklist, to ADD, if BTL LO indication goes away then.... clarifying the expected actions.
1761946: Operating flight as Pilot Monitoring. We were deviating to avoid weather along the route. We were cleared direct to ZZZZZ waypoint and asked for a deviation around weather but was initially denied. We were only authorized a deviation right of course in which were able to avoid the first TCU (Towering Cumulus) but the wind direction and velocity forced us into the second TCU as we were turning back onto course. Prior to entering the TCU the wings were leveled and we experienced a climb of approximately 700-800 ft. During the altitude excursion ATC asked why we had deviated and I replied that we were currently in the TCU. The autopilot remained engaged and within approximately 10 seconds the aircraft recovering back to the assigned altitude. ATC asked again for the reason and I replied that we had entered the TCU momentarily and was back on course and assigned altitude. ATC inability to provide deviations in either direction due to weather. Better communication between ATC facilities and increased tolerances left or right of course for hazardous weather conditions.
1761950: Momentarily exceeded flap speed for flaps one due to turbulent air in the area.While descending and slowing shortly after a moderate turbulence event the flaps one speed was briefly exceeded.Give more of an airspeed buffer in turbulent weather. FO was flying pilot. While descending into ZZZZ and deviating around convective activity, FO checked airspeed and called for flaps 1. Shortly thereafter, speed increased into the zipper. Maybe 5 knots but no more than 10.FO had not flown in a long time, lacked confidence and called for flaps way too early in an effort to get down and slow down.FO needs to fly more.
1761957: At cruise amber alert R forward window heat. Completed checklist. The outer window pane shattered. Called Dispatch and Maintenance. Diverted to ZZZ. Picked up another aircraft and continued to ZZZZ.Cause: window heat failure. I was the Relief Pilot on break when I was asked to go to the cockpit by the A FA. He had received this request from the cockpit. The right front outer windshield pane was cracked/shattered. The Captain and First Officer coordinated with Dispatch and we continued to ZZZ where we landed on Runway XXR without incident.
