1762902: I was called out on a reserve callout to deadhead to ZZZ to pickup an airplane that needed to be repositioned to ZZZ1. I noticed in the Maintenance log that Maintenance had been working on the standby Airspeed Indicator/Altimeter. I assume that this is why the airplane was stranded in ZZZ. First Officer and I completed our preflight checks and briefings to include the Non Routine Flight Operations task cards per normal, with nothing unusual occurring. We taxied out to ZZZ Runway XX, and departed normally via the ODP. The winds on takeoff were a strong gusty crosswind to about 30 knots from the right. The takeoff roll was normal with no abnormalities. We called positive rate, and then I called for 'Gear Up'. Shortly after selecting the landing gear up, all of my air data instruments went blank, and displayed Red IAS, ALT, & V/S flags. The autopilot was not engaged, and my flight director did not indicate with the loss of air data indications. I told my First Officer that I lost my airspeed and air data, and left the power set for takeoff and pitched for 10 degrees nose up. My First Officer read out the speeds on his speed tape and the standby gauges. While I had a hunch that his indications were correct, due to the Maintenance write-ups and recent work, and the unusual and immediate failure, we elected to initially diagnose this as an unreliable airspeed emergency, at least until we could verify that both the First Officer's ADC and the standby gauges were correctly indicating. I suspected an ADC 1 failure of some sorts. After reaching a safe altitude and completing the After Takeoff Checklist, I transferred the flight controls over to my First Officer, and told him to climb on course initially while we could work to verify that the airspeed indicators on his side were correctly indicating. ATC was notified of the instrument failure and of our request to climb on course for the time being. We were in VMC conditions and felt it was safe and prudent to continue to climb away from the terrain around ZZZ. As the airplane was empty, it's climb performance was exceptional. After verifying our speed, power settings, and pitch attitudes using the charts from the Unreliable Airspeed procedure we were able to affirmatively establish that both the First Officer's indications along with our standby instruments were indicating correctly. We at this point elected to abandon the unreliable airspeed procedure, as we still had two functioning airspeed indicators and instead address this as an ADC 1 abnormal procedure and failure. I felt that the unreliable airspeed procedure, while providing us with good situational information to verify that our other two indicators were functioning correctly, was irrelevant because we didn't have varying unreliable airspeed indications, but rather a complete loss of air data information. Although I suspected it was simply an ADC failure initially, due to our low altitude and critical phase of flight, we elected to initially treat the failure as an unreliable airspeed situation to assure that we were flying a safe pitch and power setting regardless of airspeed to reach a safe altitude clear of the terrain. ATC was updated that we suspected an ADC 1 failure. An emergency was never declared with ATC. We spoke to Dispatch and agreed that with the ADC 1 failure a diversion to the nearest suitable airport was not necessarily required, which is an important difference from the unreliable airspeed procedure, although we did discuss as a crew and with Dispatch the possibility of a diversion to ZZZ2 or another nearby airport along our route. We agreed that with the situation stable and well diagnosed, we felt it was pertinent, legal, and safest to continue on to ZZZ1. We landed in ZZZ1 where the ADC failure was written up in the Maintenance log as a discrepancy, and Maintenance was briefed on the phone. I called the Flight Dispatcher and debriefed with him as well, and he assured me that he was in agreement with our decision making and the [Dispatcher] was aware of the situation, and no further calls or reports were required. Maintenance later removed, and replaced ADC 1, prior to dispatching the aircraft on it's next flight. The cause of this event was a failure of ADC 1. I am curios as to whether or not the Maintenance work done on the standby airspeed/altimeter could have contributed to the failure of ADC 1. In terms of recurrence, and preventing this, from a flight ops standpoint I'm not sure what to recommend. However, I will say that this is the 2nd time in a month I have dealt with an unreliable airspeed issue, pitot/static issue, or ADC issue on the CRJ. Maybe I'm snakebit, but I have taken notice to the increase in frequency with these events. We train for this, and just a week ago I went through [training]. In our training we ran through the unreliable airspeed procedure. Because of this, I was familiar that if an initial climb is required, or just after takeoff, in the CRJ200 the checklist tells you to pitch to 10 degrees nose up at takeoff power. Fortunately, the recent familiarity with that procedure 100% helped, and was highly effective through the initial diagnosis and trouble shooting of our abnormality. There isn't a great checklist for 'loss of airspeed' in the QRH, you have to pick between unreliable airspeed, and an ADC failure. We used the Immediate Action Items from the unreliable airspeed checklist, along with the pitch/thrust reference tables, to help assure that we were climbing in a safe flight path state, and that our remaining operational airspeed indicators were properly functioning, however, then rediagnosed the issue as a full ADC 1 failure, and felt it was more prudent to treat this as an ADC failure as opposed to an unreliable airspeed emergency. I realize today though that in real life...It could be difficult to truly distinguish between the two. As a crew, we elected to start with the ultra safe option, and then once we gathered more information about the problem, were able to move into a different, and more accurate checklist, that more appropriately addressed the problem. If I could make a recommendation, I think that we need to add both memory items, and a QRC checklist for a suspected Unreliable airspeed or loss of airspeed immediate response. The immediate action items in the QRH, should absolutely be committed to memory, and probably be backed up by a QRC. While I was fortunately familiar with these, should we have a new Captain/ First Officer pairing on the aircraft in the future, that maybe isn't familiar with the aircrafts normal performance, this could potentially be an unforgivable consequence. Just a recommendation after taking some time to look back at the events of today.
1762928: We were holding short of RWY 16 at XNA. [An aircraft] had just been cleared for take off on a runway heading. Additionally, there was an aircraft inbound about 7 miles out on the ILS 16. We were then cleared for take off via the Highfill 8 turn heading 180.METAR at the time: XNA 08005KT 4SM -RA BR SCT005 OVC040 17/16 A3017 I was the Non Flying Pilot and during the take roll, I noticed radar showed moderate rain (yellow) at the 180 heading. Once airborne and before the 400 feet heading call, I asked the tower for runway heading to avoid the weather. Tower approved the runway heading and at approximately 2,500 feet to 3,000 feet we received a Terrain Terrain alert. I looked first at my Radar Altimeter which was reading and flickering between 0 and - 5, our altitude was now over 3,000 feet, and we were climbing over 1500 FPM. I stated I thought it was a spurious error, but due to the marginal weather conditions the First Officerfollowed his instincts and went to Max Thrust. At about 4,000 feet I pulled up the ILS 34 Jepp chart and noted a Tower 1,855 feet SE of the Localizer and about 8 km SE of the airport. I also noted that our GPS position was showing on this chart and we were on the outbound LOC course. Additionally, there is no Obstacle DP for RWY 16 on the 20-9 page. I still believe this was a spurious Radar Atl error but while troubleshooting I may have distracted the First Officerfrom making the Terrain Max Thrust call. Considering the marginal visual conditions I should have stated Terrain instead of Troubleshooting. We tookoff at XNA on Runway 16. Just after takeoff, as per the departure procedure we were supposed to turn right to 180 heading. Right at about 400 feet, when I'm supposed to call heading, the Captain asked ATC for runway heading to avoid some bad weather. ATC gave us runway heading and the Captain turned the heading bug to runway heading and selected HDG. At about 1,000 feet, I called Vnav. Then at about 3,000 feet, we had a terrain alert, 'Too low terrain.' I was a little startled by the alert, and thought it must have been an erroneous alert and was somewhat confused because of it. I did pitch up a little more due to the alert, but I did not go max thrust and do a proper terrain escape procedure, even though I still should have.After pitching up a little more for a few seconds I noticed the speed start to drop which I stated to the Captain, and thinking that I should have just done the proper procedure, I then went to max thrust. He stated to just lower the nose a little bit, at which point I did, and then pulled the thrust levers back out of max thrust and started to go into the recovery. The speed started to come back up, and then I called for flaps 1, and flaps up. We switched over to the departure frequency, and then I asked him for the auto throttle back on, and the autopilot on. The flight continued normally without any further incidents. Once we were all cleaned up and climbing properly, we looked over the charts, to see what could have caused the terrain alert. It is not a mountainous terrain airport and the elevation all looks constant. There looks to be one obstacle that may have caused it that goes up to 1,855 feet about 8 miles SE of the field. Both the Captain and I seemed to believe that it was a false indication for the alert, because an [aircraft] took off a few minutes before we did, and the tower told them to fly runway heading right after they were airborne, which I doubt tower would have given them if there were obstacles or terrain in the way. Because we thought it was a false indication was why we did not do a proper escape and recovery, which is not a good excuse. Next time I will be sure to do a proper procedure, no matter what I may think or feel.

1762974: I want to take the opportunity to express my concerns regarding pitot tubes covers and inspection requirements and that is...here at ZZZ we have airplanes that sit on ground for more than XX hours and therefore need pitot inspections before departure as the GPM XX.XX.X states and are accomplished...our concerns rely on the fact that these same airplanes are not scheduled to depart until most of times well beyond a substantial period of time on ground and as mechanics we feel that signing the pitot inspections well before hours (i.e., 4 hours, 6 hours, 8 hours, etc.) before departure is a safety concern because these same aircrafts are sitting on remote pads of the airport without pitot covers since ZZZ has no covers available or NOT enough!! 1763018: I was flying (Aircraft X) as wingman in a formation of 2 aircraft. The lead aircraft (Aircraft Y) was in contact with PWM Approach for flight following while we were in cruise at 4,500 MSL. I was speaking to my lead on 123.45 and squawking standby at the request of ATC. As we were about to overfly the PWM Class C airspace, we suddenly saw a CRJ immediately off my left wing and what I would estimate as maybe 200-300 vertical separation. The aircraft was close enough that I was easily able to read '[Company]' on the side of the aircraft. I was unaware at the time of the traffic as I was not personally speaking to Approach controllers. After the event, I called PWM Approach on the telephone to discuss it and make sure no action was needed. The controller stated that we had 500 feet separation and nothing was needed from us.Later, after speaking with my Lead Pilot, and listening to audio of the ATC from liveatc.net we were able to piece together what had happened. The [commercial] flight had been cleared up to 4,000 feet on their climb, presumably to provide separation from us at 4,500 feet. My Lead Pilot had been given a traffic alert by approach and the same had been done to the [commercial] flight for us. My Lead Pilot reported them in sight after they were already past us as neither of us saw them until the last second. No evasive action was needed. We did later find out from the ATC audio that they had received an RA (Resolution Advisory) from their TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) system which they reported to the Controller. The controllers did not tell me this when we spoke on the phone. The largest concern from this event is that we had been instructed about 10 minutes prior to the event to maintain VFR at or above 3,500 feet, and the [commercial] flight had been cleared to climb through the altitude restriction that we had been given. Had we decided to start a descent from 4,500 feet at any point between then and the miss between us and the [commercial] aircraft, the results would likely have been much different. It is our opinion that the [commercial] aircraft was not in 500 feet separation from us, although that is a visual judgement and cannot be confirmed. We do not know if they exceeded their cleared altitude. To the best of our knowledge no formal reporting is being performed by [commercial], ourselves, or ATC.

1763036: Military Special Use airspace can be scheduled by different user's facilities. When we entered the airspace NOTAMs into the system, a conflict alert was generated and apparently some work was done by the swing shift yesterday to track down the problem. However they were unable to locate the email from a month prior and assumed it was entered into the system in error. They cancelled the first request and entered the second request into the schedule. The first facility was unaware their schedule was removed and thought they still had the airspace scheduled. It wasn't until this morning that a Center Oceanic sector noticed the discrepancy and hour before the events and questioned who actually was going to have the airspace. Fortunately we were able to notify the users and cancel one of the missions in time, however this was lucky and was a potentially very dangerous situation.The way Warning Area schedules are sent to the MOS is confusing and inconsistent. We should only receive airspace activation from one entity and only on the day prior. Because the schedules come in different formats and at different times, it is hard (if not impossible) to track and catch errors. Furthermore it should not be the role of the MOS to catch and referee scheduling errors especially since Center is not the scheduling agency for this airspace. At a minimum consistent forms should be used for all airspace schedules (which would help the MOS catch any errors) and ideally we should only receive the schedule from NAWC [Naval Air War Center] along with the other daily airspace schedules we receive from them.

1763147: The event occurred on a flight between ZZZ and ZZZ1. We had been delayed multiple times at our base of operations due to mechanical issues and eventually were switched to a different aircraft that became available late in the day. Throughout the rescheduling and refiling/updating flight plans we had taken consideration of our duty time and had set a latest takeoff time from base that would allow us to complete our flights and return to base before the end of our duty time. However in all that I failed to consider night landing currency for carrying passengers. It was not until after we had picked up our passenger and were enroute to ZZZ1 and the sun had set that the FO (pilot flying) looked at me and said that he couldn't make the landing as he was not night current. Then I realized I was not night current either. At this point we realized it was too late and continued to our destination. I had the FO do the landing which in retrospect as PIC I should have shown more initiative in taking full responsibility by taking the landing instead of putting the FO in the position of making a landing out of currency.A contributing factor is that in the past I have seldom carried passengers for my employer. Most often I am doing other type of flying with only required crew on board due to the aircraft being in the restricted category. But I have more recently been doing an occasional passenger carrying flight where I have to think about passenger carrying currency more. Also due to economic slow down there has been less opportunity to keep up currency especially night currency with our normal operations. For corrective actions I have made a checklist for myself that goes in my knee board specifically for passenger carrying flights, because they are so infrequent, that lists the pertinent things that should be considered during pre-flight and more specifically the more pertinent things like passenger carrying currency. This will be a checklist that I see when I open my knee board prior to flight and work through at the latest, just before engine start.

1763161: On practice ZZZ LOC XX, approximately 4 miles from the end of the runway, flight in VFR conditions above an undercast we received a low altitude alert from ZZZ Tower. We advised Tower were VFR and leveling at the MDA (900 MSL) and, at the same time, while cross checking our position on the LOC both pilots noted that the GPS had not updated from the Final Approach Fix (ZZZZZ) to the end of the runway. After cross checking position on the EFB display we elected to execute a missed approach at the end of the runway.The reason for this report is both systems and human factors related. Both pilots were concentrating on the descent and level off from FAF altitude to MDA using a 'dive and drive procedure' which is no longer commonly used in heavy jet aircraft. Concentrating on the altitude an equipment error to update the next waypoint automatically was missed and the low altitude alert from Tower compounded the 'startle factor'. The startle factor was amplified by the fact we were VFR above an overcast with no terrain in sight. Based on training, we executed a missed approach to create time and regain situational awareness, from a personal perspective when an unexpected event occurs, even in seasoned pilots, it takes a few minutes to understand what happened, not second guess yourself and reset situational awareness.As a follow-up to the event, I contacted ZZZ Tower who related that they have issued numerous low altitude alerts on this approach, for aircraft at the correct altitude, usually involving a high descent rate approach to MDA. I reviewed the approach with the PF (Pilot Flying)and confirmed that he had set an excessive rate (1500 feet/min) when our company procedure calls for less than 1,000 feet/min within 1,000 feet of the terrain.A better briefing on use of automation during the crew brief may have mitigated the high descent rate, and as Pilot Not Flying validating the waypoint switch over at FAF should have been accomplished. Although we were given missed approach instructions ahead of time from approach control (practice approach), if we were relying on GPS for the published missed, it would have been difficult to reprogram the GPS (during the missed approach) to fly the published missed approach (our aircraft does not have TACAN (Tactical Air Navigation system) (raw data) capability and in this situation would require GPS to fly the published missed). As a final observation, we did not receive any onboard GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) or TAWS (Terrain Avoidance and Warning System) warning with respect to terrain and have asked company maintenance to verify proper operation of both systems.
1763184: My student on his second solo landed and veered off the runway about 5 feet during the attempt to do a touch and go. His approach was stable and landing was on centerline. There are a couple factors that I believe led to this runway excursion. First, I believe he rushed into taking off after landing, without taking the time to ensure the flaps were up and that the aircraft was still under control. Second, I believe he accidentally applied more left rudder than he had intended causing him to veer off to the left of the runway. After applying full power he began to veer to the left of the runway. He corrected for this by pulling back power and applying right rudder, but not fast enough to prevent momentarily veering off the runway. Too much rudder control causing veer off the left of the runway. No damage or injuries.
1763187: Very clear, minimal winds. AWOS (Automated Weather Observing System) - Calm winds. Monitoring [radio] all runways were being utilized. Calm wind preferred Runway is XX/XY. I depressed my brakes as hard as possible, maintained directional control, while deciding whether I should deviate to the left or right. The C-172 decelerated and turned into the grass between taxiway C and runway XY soon coming to a complete stop. Aircraft Y called out warning of event on radio. 1763189: After lifting off Runway XX, I retracted the gear, allowed the aircraft to accelerate to 120 knots and was about to retract the takeoff flaps setting. The Tower cleared me to a right turn for my westerly heading, when suddenly there was a loud noise and a strong rush of air as the canopy departed. I looked at my ground position and airspeed. I added power called the Tower and informed them of the situation and asked to return. I continued climbing to pattern altitude. Tower cleared me to land. I waited until my base turn to lower the gear. On short final I added full flaps. I kept the airspeed about 10 knots higher than normal (100 knots). Landed and taxied to hanger. I plan on making a checklist that you have to check off each box before moving on, and continue going to safety seminars as I had for years.
1763191: I was watching a trainee in the Local Control position when ground/flight data/clearance delivery passed inbound information from ZZZ ARTCC of Aircraft X two miles south east of the airport for a visual approach to Runway XX. This created a dangerous situation with very little time to react or plan, especially with a trainee who was on day 4 of re-entering training after six months plus of not working local due to COVID and me not training anyone for just as long if not longer due to COVID.Follow the LOA between ZZZ ARTCC and ZZZ Tower. I was training on local, which I had not worked local in about 6 months due to the COVID pandemic, it was my fourth day back into training. Shortly thereafter Aircraft X calls me about one to two miles northeast of the field saying he is on a visual approach to Runway XX. I asked Aircraft X how long he would need to continue north before he would turn base in which he told me about another mile and then he would turn his base. I acknowledged him and told him to report turning base. I then started moving aircraft out of the way and sequencing aircraft behind him in order to make it work. Being that I had not got a position on Aircraft X when I noticed him so close to the airport on the STARS, I was under the impression that center was vectoring the aircraft for an RNAV XX approach only to find out last minute that the aircraft was going to be doing a visual approach to XX and then I was not given any time to build a gap to fit the aircraft into.In accordance with the LOA between ZZZ Tower and ZZZ Center, the Center is supposed to call with a position on inbound aircraft with a type of approach to expect. My recommendation is for center to follow the LOA and inbound the aircraft sooner, allowing tower time to build gaps for IFR aircraft.

1763209: I accepted the hand-off on Aircraft X from ZZZ approach and put a PVD (Plan View Display) on what I thought was ZZZ Approach LO's scope. 1763225: This could be called a systemic problem, as it happens all the time. I filed it as an event since you can specifically look at this event. Aircraft X departed and did not tag up. 1763302: 3rd day of flying. 3rd flight of day. We had set up for the ILS Approach in accordance with ATIS. No mention was made of Visual Approaches being in use. Despite that fact, we briefed the restrictions over a satellite airport as a precaution.We were taken off the RNAV Arrival and were given a series of step down clearances as we approached the field. Simultaneously, we were told to expect the RNAV Visual Approach. The Pilot Monitoring loaded the new approach as we were below 10,000 ft. which I as the Pilot Flying rapidly briefed. Shortly thereafter, we were cleared to a point not on the arrival nor the RNAV Visual. As the Pilot Monitoring began searching for the fix, I maintained a 3:1 descent rate via VSpeed/Open Des. I was also approaching the point where I was going to need to configure if I wished to have a stabilized approach. The Pilot Monitoring found the fix on the RNAV (GPS) Approach and raced to reconfigure the FMS. Then, having given no prior warning, the Approach Controller cleared us for the ILS Approach which would have been impossible at this point. Having the runway in sight and fearing that any further 'assistance' from the controller would do little to aid my rapidly deteriorating situational awareness, I elected to disconnect the autopilot, and fly the approach visually. I pulled my Pilot Monitoring back into the loop by asking for him to clear my flight directors, configure the aircraft, and ask approach for the Visual Approach. The controller cleared us for the Visual Approach, 'as long as we fly the glideslope down', which I'd submit is not a legal clearance, but was in any case irrelevant as following the glideslope had always been our intention. After doing some fishing to configure the aircraft and get down onto glideslope, the Pilot Monitoring reselected the approach and flight directors and we flew a stabilized approach to landing. In debriefing this event, we discovered that the fix was also present on the ILS Approach, which was the approach that ATIS had specified, the approach that we had initially briefed, and presumably the approach that the controller wished us to fly all along. I can't say what the Approach controller was thinking during this event. However, on an approach as infamous as any to I can only suggest that last minute changes are inappropriate and unsafe. I also think that the controller has an inaccurate impression of what is required of aircrews when changing approaches. I would suggest that the reality of flying this approach be made clear to her as controlling that is this cavalier will only lead to further unstabilized approaches in the future, or worse. The last minute change to the RNAV Visual followed by clearing us to a point not on the approach, followed by a second clearance for the ILS risked completely overwhelming the aircrew. That this was on a runway that is notorious for unstabilized approaches only exacerbated matters. Frankly, any acceptance of other than ILS approaches to this runway should be disallowed. Flying Visual Approaches to this runway, with it's unique peculiarities is a procedure designed by ATC, for the benefit of ATC. By definition and data, flying this Visual Approach is a compromise of safety for the sake of expediency, and sets aircrew up to be 'the last line of defense', with generally predictable results.

1763319: While executing a visual approach to Runway XX ZZZ airport, I was on a proper visual glide path until approximately 1/2 - 1/4 mile final. A breakdown in my scan resulted in descending below a normal glide path, as a result we were unstable below 500 feet AGL. Neither pilot called for a go-around, though, after debrief it was agreed that a go-around would have been appropriate. I was able to correct back on profile, approximately at 1/4 mile short final. The landing was safe, on speed and uneventful.Contributing factors included light turbulence requiring constant power adjustments. Also, lack of recent flight time due to taking leave--this was my first approach/landing in a number of weeks on top of very limited flight time in the past 6 months. Additionally, as experienced from the previous ILS approach to the same runway conducted earlier the same day, it was noticed that while on or above glide path, the PAPI's indicated well below, despite glide slope and VGSI not being coincident per the procedure. The note on the procedure indicated that the VGSI would bring the aircraft across the threshold at approximately 50 feet, however, coming across the threshold at 80 feet, the PAPI's still indicated low (one white over three red). This issue was briefed to be mitigated by referencing altitude/distance check points on descent, however, it still became an issue. The lack of proper visual guidance may have contributed to a departure from a stable glide path, however, did not contribute to the failure to call a go-around. The PAPI guidance issue was brought to the attention of the airport manager.The potential lack of flight time/currency due to COVID is a potential universal issue. I have a luxury of flying with the X Group to maintain a scan but for those that don't, a severely reduced schedule will likely result in some loss of proficiency. A solution may be to promote those with reduced flying to take more legs/landings than normal within a given pairing. Additionally, aside from notifying the airport or ATC of malfunctioning equipment, e.g., PAPI's, there should be a means by which to relay this information to the company for immediate communication to air crew, as there is no guarantee of a swift response or fix. (aside from NOTAMs). Was pilot monitoring. We were coming in to land on the visual to Runway XX in ZZZ. During the last 1/4 to 1/2 mile on the approach. The pilot flying misjudged the distance and descent rate during the approach and started to get low on the approach. Pilot flying corrected but we were unstabilized on the approach and did not execute a go-around. We landed from the approach without incident within the touchdown zone area on the runway. The pilot flying had not been flying very much recently so lack of recent experience was a factor. A failure of the pilot monitoring to call for a go-around from an unstable approach. A failure of the pilot flying to call for a go-around from an unstabilized approach. Complacency on approach and not wanting to inconvenience passengers. Poor decision making by pilots.As pilots we have to always remember safety is top priority. Even if it's an inconvenience to both [of] you and everyone on board. If an approach becomes unstabalized a go-around or missed approach must be executed. Even if the landing happens safely and the landing is 'salvaged' it's important to remember that one day it might not be. As a pilot monitoring if you see an unstabilized approach you should speak up. Don't worry about hurt feelings. Missed connections. We can't get complacent and think that we can just continue from an unstabilized approach.

While running the QRH for that at approximately 7,500 ft., the windshield cracked. We immediately stopped climbing and slowed to 200 kts. and requested a turn back to the airport while running the QRH for that. The windshield really wasn't a problem. The issue was when after I turned off the autopilot for the Visual Approach, I noticed right away that the flight controls felt strange. They seemed to be much less effective mostly in pitch. I was having a hard time staying in the flight director because it felt like I was having to make large inputs with delayed response from the plane. We were able to land safely. I wrote up that the controls were spongy less responsive. We went to the hotel. In the morning, I called maintenance to ask what they had found. I was told that they checked the cables and pulleys and that nothing was found. I told the maintenance controller that I wasn't going to fly it until something was found. We went to the hangar in the morning a bit early so I could talk to the maintenance team. I saw that the logbook was signed off and that it indicated 'flight control check satisfactory', and it was signed off. I told my concerns to a few mechanics. Some didn't seem real concerned. A couple were curious. I took one to another aircraft in the hangar and had him do a flight control check. Then went back to my plane and did one. He immediately said 'wow, this one is much harder, and I feel a catch in the elevator'. He said that is definitely the pitch feel system and the plane was then put back on maintenance to get fixed. My concern is that if another crew had been assigned to this plane, they might've not noticed the odd feeling flight control check and tried to go flying with potentially bad results. Flight control concerns from pilots need to be taken seriously! The First Officer who was in the right seat and did the flight control check, said they felt fine when he did the check before takeoff.I suggest Maintenance take major issues such as flight control concerns from pilots more seriously. I also suggest the mechanic that signed the plane off get more training. Their procedures for flight control checks might need to change. Another aircraft should've been used as an example to see if the problem aircraft felt the same.
1763378: I am working C position on this flight. I briefed the OWWE (Over Wing Window Exit) and all were in compliance. My A FA, upon doing her final walk through for takeoff had to tell passenger seated XX2 to stow her bag back under the seat in front of her. Passenger in doing so FA A noticed she was wearing a small boot on her left foot. FA A informed the pilots we had to re-seat passenger. Pilots pulled over, passenger was reseated and we went on our way.I do not know the exact time of day this happened, but was told we arrived 5 minutes late. But it says differently on our payroll sheet which says we arrived early. With that being said, we had a few mask situations during descent, one passenger complaining another wasn't wearing her mask, both passenger were through passenger. Announcements were made, 2 of the 4 FAs spoke to the unmasked passenger. During cleaning of aircraft a passenger informed me of the passenger not wearing her mask. I spoke to the unmasked passenger explaining why she had to wear a mask, but we ended up requesting either Operations or a Supervisor to speak to unmasked passenger because she told me the old lady needs to mind her own business. Operations agent took unmasked passenger to jetway to talk and situation was resolved. Unmasked passenger sat YY4 the complaining passenger moved fwd about row XD. Now we're boarding. One passenger tried to sit in OWWE using a seatbelt extension, passengers were letting their masks fall below their nose, a passenger received a call and took her mask off while walking through cabin, I got her attention by stepping into the aisle and put my hand in front of my face. She understood what I was getting at, she stopped, put her mask back on and was apologetic. Both the D & I had heavy mask patrol that flight. While briefing my OWWE I never noticed the boot wearing lady's foot with boot. All items were stowed.
1763379: Passenger would not wear appropriate face cover and became confrontational. The event escalated to the point I had a stress related ocular migraine and was forced to call out sick from the aircraft and seek medical attention. In the event I possibly broke a minimum crew regulation by not waiting for a crew member replacement before attaining medical attention.
1763385: Flight wasn't full. Agents unblocked seats at X2 and X5. Social distancing for my jumpseat policy violated.
1763387: Passengers blatantly refused to wear masks. Masks must be worn at all times, even while sleeping in flight. The only time the masks can be removed is while actively eating or drinking. This was the most non-compliant flight to date. There were passengers only covering their mouth and not their nose. There were many passengers who didn't have a mask on at all. When we would ask them to put a mask on they would roll their eyes, pretend to put it on and take it off as soon as we walked away. We all have families to go home to. This is not acceptable. Every other airline firmly enforces the mask policy.Enforce the mask wearing policy strictly for all passengers and all airline crew, including mechanics, flight attendants, grounds ops personnel and pilots.
1763397: The passenger in seat X1 kept pulling his mask down, he did comply but kept doing it. He was also agitated when we told him we needed his mask to cover his nose and mouth. We were kind about it too. At one point he claimed to have a health condition. It did not say anything in the paper work of mask/face covering exemptions. I informed the other Flight Attendant and she agreed to let the flight deck know. The flight deck asked if he had been verbally aggressive towards us. He had not. The flight deck had a [CSR] meet the plane. We talked to [CSR] because the passenger told them we were rude and we were not. [CSR] told us we handled it perfectly.
1763404: Passenger X was wearing a face shield without a mask. I noticed during boarding process. I informed him policy is to wear a face mask over his nose and mouth as well. He said for me to stop talking to him and go away. He said he had a condition. He repeated, that he wanted me to go away and stop talking to [him]. I asked him if he had talked to an agent? He said there was no one to talk to at the gate. I offered for him to talk to a gate agent. He again said for me to go away and did not want to talk to me. He appeared to be pulling a mask out of his bag, as I was offering to go get one for him. The FA C came and [offered] some masks. He told her to go away. Next time I was in the aisle about 10 minutes later, he had the mask on but below his nose and mouth. I asked him to make sure he had his mask pulled up, he was hostile and said he was not going to speak to me. Told me to 'Go away, I'm not talking to you.' I informed the A FA, she informed the CA. They decided to remove the passenger. An employee flying in Row XX witnessed the exchange. He was not in compliance and a safety hazard to other passengers and crew for COVID-19.
1763408: I am suggesting that an investigation is launched into the possibility of contract aircraft cleaners unknowingly scratching aircraft windshields while performing their duties. After thinking more about the Tech Ops Update and a recent CBT (Computer Based Training) on 737 Windshield scratching I wonder if the uptick in B737 windshield replacements is from non-certificated individuals inadvertently imposing damage to the windshields. I am not sure what method the cleaners use, what cleaning agents, what type of cloth, etc. Do the materials conform to the Boeing Maintenance Manual? Not pointing a finger here, but just thinking that we may have an opportunity to reduce inadvertent damage to the windshields here if we initiate a change management process. Again, the cleaners are just doing what they believe is their job, but it may have been an oversight that we (company) requested them to clean the windshields, or didn't realize that they were cleaning the aircraft windshields, potentially using a damaging process, chemical or consumable item (rags, paper towels, etc.).
1763410: Sorry to have come to you for issues pertaining to night shift but we as Aircraft Maintenance Technicians feel the need to write to you all as our requests to night shift supervisors have gone into one ear and come out the other without any interest to these issues. As you all probably know we at nights perform different checks and routine maintenance on the airplanes sitting out there on the remote pads. We have expressed our concerns to night shift supervisors about the need to add more entry door Stairs/Stands...for Aircraft X/Y types as well as Lighting Fixtures since it's completely dark at night.Now that more airplanes are being parked, what do we have to do so that our requests/concerns are answered? Answers Supervisors like to say like 'We just gotta work around these issues' are not of people with sound judgment...hence as working group we felt the need to write to you all to explore better possibilities to these specific issues. Again these are safety concerns we feel need to be address as more planes are being parked in these remote areas we need more lighting fixtures and as well as entry door stairs to better accomplish all the required work assigned.Need management to provide us with entry door stands.
1763411: While dispatching two aircraft at the same time last night we had an APU door fault on one of the aircraft. While filling out the MEL log item and placard for the APU door message I filled out the log page and started to sign off item and got involved adding a statement to the yellow placard requested by maintenance control. I forgot to come back to that log page and put my signature, I had the date filled out but missed the signature. It was an error on my part trying to get a flight crew out before they timed out. I was trying to comply with too many tasks at one time. Had two departures at the same time and a deadline. Take more time and attention to task at hand. A Fuel door recycling Airworthiness Directive (AD) was complied with but the misc. 91 was not sent correctly. We were unaware that there was required text that was supposed to be sent along with the misc 91. This was a relatively new AD and the specifics of compliance were confusing. Since neither the First Officer or I had flown since this AD came out, the fact that wording was supposed to accompany the misc 91 was missed. It would be nice if the exact steps required were readily available in the logbook or somewhere handy during the preflight.
1763430: We were flying to ZZZ, assigned the XX LDA starting at ZZZ1 VOR. We were instructed to cross ZZZ1 VOR at or above 15,000 and cleared for the approach. We had programmed the avionics to fly the approach and descend on the approach to the glide slope intercept altitude. During the setup we neglected to arm the VNAV. After passing ZZZ1, descending, the aircraft did not level off at 14,000. We noticed the missed level off just before the controller alerted us to a probable altitude deviation. The Captain immediately disconnected the autopilot and returned to the appropriate altitude. The flight concluded uneventfully.I believe there were several factors that contributed to the event. Primarily, the flight crew was legally current but a little out of practice. A full procedure instrument approach in real-time in mountainous terrain is different than currency and maintenance flights in non mountainous terrain. We have a very strong safety culture, attend recurrent training more frequently than required, and have extensive backgrounds including airline and corporate jet experience but are still susceptible to being 'rusty'.
1763441: I was riding along with an owner in his experimental aircraft. The weather conditions were VFR, however, visibility was somewhat reduced due to likely smoke/haze and light scatter in the area. Departed normally from ZZZ and headed northwest bound. Listened to ATIS and contacted Approach control and indicated our intentions for continued northwest bound flight for their awareness. We were not planning to fly near ZZZ1 airport, but the airspace is very busy within approximately 30 nm of the field, so participating in traffic advisories is good practice. Typically, TRACON would provide a squawk code and RADAR identification, however, this evening approach control responded to our request and stated 'aircraft calling in, maintain VFR'. As the airspace was very busy with multiple VFR and IFR aircraft during this time, we took this response from ATC as 'we're not interested in another VFR aircraft' particularly since we were not directly arriving into or departing from ZZZ1 airport itself. Despite this response from ATC, we continued to monitor ZZZ1 approach frequency on 132.3. We leveled-off at 4,500 ft. MSL continued flying northwest bound. Approximately 10-15 mins later, about 5-8 nm south of ZZZ2 airport when we noticed potential conflict traffic on the aircraft's MFD and through the Foreflight App with ADS-B in. Using technology, we noticed the aircraft was flying directly towards us and climbing into our altitude, with altitude difference noted as 500, 400, 300, etc. below and difference decreasing. We attempted to establish visual contact with the aircraft, cross-referencing the iPad display and MFD. The aircraft was noted crossing under our right wing, approximately 300-400 ft. before we noticed the aircraft. Although we were monitoring Approach, it was unclear what instructions the other aircraft was provided regarding our position. In either case, the other aircraft was closer than I typically prefer, without prior coordination. Later on that same flight, we contacted Center to request flight following for the return leg through the ZZZ1 airspace. Center provided us a squawk code, then a few minutes later stated 'Aircraft X, I seem to have lost your altitude squawk, state your altitude.' As we were now returning and southeast bound, I responded with 'Aircraft X, level, five-thousand five hundred.' After receiving this call from ATC, I queried the aircraft owner to see if the transponder 'ALT' reporting was selected on through his MFD. Upon checking, it appeared the transponder was 'ON' but had inadvertently been selected out of the 'ALT' squawk mode. It is possible this inadvertent selection could have contributed to the earlier potential traffic hazard witnessed earlier in the flight. I discussed the setting with the owner and indicated that the transponder should be left in the 'ALT' setting continuously (unless otherwise requested by ATC). We continued uneventfully for the remainder of the flight, despite very active ATC communications, active vectoring and traffic avoidance while returning in and through the airspace into ZZZ. The vectoring, traffic avoidance and unexpected headwinds upon the return slightly delayed our arrival into ZZZ, however, we landed uneventfully. On way to Walhalla area from ZZZ to look at fall colors noticed an aircraft from UND Aerospace on a general track towards us at about 1000 ft below our altitude. I believe they were also changing course somewhat also. We monitored as the distance closed. We were on autopilot at 4500 ft MSL and on course of 320. As the other plane closed to 1-2 mi. they began to climb. They seemed to level off about 500 ft. below us but just before our paths crossed they climbed to an estimated 300 ft. below us. My plane is equipped with ADS-B in and out. I was accompanied by my son-in-law who is a CFI. Later in the flight he noticed that the transponder was set to ON not ALT. Because of this I am not sure if the other aircraft was receiving information on our altitude. In hind sight we should have altered our course to avoid crossing like this. I believe this was an instance where having two pilots was a factor in not taking action. In the past when flying with my wife, I have taken action to maneuver around another aircraft in a similar situation. On The other hand, based on the maneuvering the other aircraft was doing it was not clear which direction we would need to go to avoid crossing paths. A lesson learned for me is to check that my transponder is set to ALT on future flights.
1763442: I was on Visual Approach backed up with the RNAV Approach. On Visual Approach had a couple big down drafts around 1500 ft. with some precipitation when I went near a big dark cloud. The rest of approach was normal. Fully configured by 1,000 ft and on speed and glide path stable approach. The winds reported were variable at 4 kts. Over the threshold began to flare and pull engine to idle, at about 15-20 ft, at 115 kts, all lift went away, felt bottom drop out of us, and aircraft dropped approximately 15 ft to runway. Control inputs did very little to correct situation to arrest the increased rate of descent. I got a big tail wind gust or got caught in a microburst of some sort. The aircraft slammed onto the runway right main first, breaking and collapsing the right main gear. I slid down runway 2,000 ft. or so before leaving the pavement to the right. No injuries. Pilot and passenger unhurt.
1763455: As I finish my descent checklist and approached to ZZZ from the East 20 NM out I got my ATIS, called ZZZ tower and reported my position. I was instructed to enter the left downwind for runway XX. As I entered the left downwind and completed my before landing checklist I called the tower to let them know my position and I was clear to land. Abeam the numbers I began configuring my flaps after I slow down to my white arc. On base I selected my second notch of flaps and slow to 80 kts, on final I configured to flaps landing and I maintained my final approach speed. On final I stay on my center line, followed the PAPI and crossing the threshold I kept my airspeed about 70 kts began my flare and landed. It wasn't until my mains touched down and the nosewheel was on the ground and on the centerline that I felt a pulled to the left. I corrected to the right to no avail. The nosewheel did not steer to the right. As the airplane slowed down it continue to pull me to the left while I attempted to correct but there was no response on the airplane's nosewheel. The aircraft's left main gear and nosewheel went off the runway. I proceeded to do my shutdown checklist followed by a call to ZZZ Tower to informed them of the event. The tower sent a vehicle to pick us up. I called the tower on the telephone number as requested to provide my information.
1763470: Attempted to load approach into Garmin 3000 touchscreen controller. Slight turbulence caused pilot to touch load/activate button. This single action changes navigation mode, auto pilot guidance, and flight plan screen. Several pilot actions are required to undo the situation, allowing aircraft to leave the designed STAR until either reverting to manual control or completing to navigation system corrections. Perhaps a function that undoes the last command would be valuable.
1763479: Shortly after takeoff at around 2,000 ft. the right wing tip tank ran out of fuel. The engine then quit. I tried the fuel pump magnetos mixture and throttle. I then squawked 7700 and advised ATC on 121.5. TRACON then contacted me on 121.5 with vectors back to my departure airport and I told them I was unable and landing on the beach. Shortly after that it occurred to me to switch the fuel tanks so I did and what felt like about 30 seconds later the engine roared back to life. I then climbed and proceeded direct to my destination and informed the controller of what I was doing. I landed safely and talked to the police and fire department that was already waiting for us on the ground.I think the contributing factors are earlier in the day was my first time flying this aircraft type in over a year. Another contributing factor is most of my recent time is in an aircraft which does not require fuel tank switching. And the last contributing factor in my opinion is that the fuel gauges were not lit. I believe if they were lit I would have seen them in my scan and noticed the low fuel in the right tip tank before it ran out.
1763482: We were on a VFR descent into the airport. Approach gave us a handoff to tower. As I was making contact with Tower a white Cessna passed underneath us by 200 to 300 feet. The traffic did not show up on the Garmin 430 and no warning was given by ATC. I suspect that the traffic did not have an operable transponder. They did not seem to notice our aircraft.
1763493: While being vectored and cleared for an on RNAV Approach as soon as frequency change was advised it was noted a plane was on runway opposite direction that cleared within 15 seconds and another that had taken runway took off at the same time. Evasive maneuver taken by me and no accident happened. As I turned eastbound another aircraft was noted to be on left base for runway 19. Three aircraft had been flying runway that winds did not favor and an accident could have occurred. I am interested in understanding what should have been done differently.
1763503: Descending to assigned altitude of 13,000 ft traffic with below at 12,000 ft. The aircraft leveled off with autopilot in alt hold at 13,000 ft. I looked down at the FMS, selected direct to assigned intersection, looked up and aircraft was in a descending right hand turn. The Co-pilot indicated autopilot had disconnected and applied back pressure to regain altitude but because of bank co-pilots back pressure increased bank from standard rate angle of bank to 45 degrees of bank. The Pilot applied unusual attitude recovery procedures. Leveled wings then increased back pressure to climb back to assigned altitude of 13,000 ft. There was a loss of 500 ft with altitude deviation.
1763520: Circling for 34 At Chicago Executive. Following a Citation Jet & Challenger Jet. Was circling for 34. Got a lot of wake turbulence behind the jets on the circling approach. Reported it to the Tower [who] suggested [I] do a 360 but because of the altitude of Class B decided not to do a 360 but wanted to stay out of the wake turbulence so could not descend below the Class Bravo. Due to the long base to final to maintain separation and avoid the jet wake [I] encroached the Class B airspace. Was aware of the fact [and] exited as soon as safely possible and landed at PWK.
1763547: Was being vectored for the GPS XX approach at ZZZ. Was a plane ahead with a similar call sign. Controller gave me a approach clearance for the ILS XX, I was expecting the GPS XX and the position sounded off. I turned to join the approach course as I was positioned for this, but then questioned the Controller telling him I thought he meant to give the clearance to the plane ahead. He said he had but the plane ahead also stated they were given no clearance.The Controller had given me, Aircraft X, the clearance in error. I then turned back to my assigned heading and the Controller then cleared the other plane. I never left my assigned altitude. The Controller seemed over loaded throughout the flight. The current staffing at ATC seems to be straining their capacity with controllers covering many more frequencies which means pilots tend to step on each other as we can't hear the other frequencies.
1763584: During the ZZZZZ X Arrival, a late clearance was issued and believed to have been to 'Expect ZZZZZ1 at 250 knots.' That 'Expect' clearance was read back by the Pilot Flying (First Officer) due to the fact that the Pilot Monitoring (Captain) was speaking to the flight attendants on the interphone. After passing ZZZZZ1, ATC asked to verify that we were at 250 knots, the First Officer/PM responded that we were awaiting the expect 250 knots clearance. The ATC Controller made reference to the fact that he was wearing a face mask and the clearance may have been miss-understood. The Captain returned from speaking with the flight attendants and the First Officer briefed him on the miss-understanding of the 'expect 250 knot' clearance. The aircraft was slowed to 250 knots and the flight continued on the ZZZZZ X Arrival uneventfully.Communication with ATC can be difficult enough. Controllers wearing face masks doesn't seem like a good idea. We were descending on the ZZZZZ X. I notified my First Officer that I would be off for a moment, so as to notify the flight attendants to take their seats due to the turbulence. When I notified my First Officer I was back, he informed me that ATC had told us to expect ZZZZZ1 intersection at 250 knots. Shortly after passing ZZZZZ1, ATC queried our speed. We notified ATC that we were at 280 knots but were never assigned the 250 knots at ZZZZZ1 that he told us to expect. ATC commented that he was wearing a face mask and that it was probably hard for us to understand him. We slowed to 250 knots and the remainder of flight was uneventful.
1763592: After an uneventful approach, landing, and taxi to the gate, we approached the J-line for our gate. While verifying that the safety zone was clear, we noticed that a provisioning truck was servicing the forward galley of the aircraft at the adjacent gate. The lower tailgate of the truck was very close to the edge of the safety zone but we determined that it was outside the line and continued. I taxied very slowly because the box of the truck looked close from my angle of sight. We did not receive any signal to stop and parked without incident. However, the wing walker came up to the cockpit to talk to us afterwards and mentioned that he noticed me looking at the wingtip, and he had the same concerns I did. He stated that the wingtip and the truck box seemed very close, approximately one foot in his estimation. He also was wondering if I could see his wand because, at that point, he and the Marshaler had no line of sight with each other due to the jetbridge. My concern is that if I am looking at the Marshaler and he cannot see the left Wing Walker in this situation, then we are essentially blind. Even though nothing happened, I feel like I should have stopped and waited for the truck to move. The Wing Walker and the rest of the Ground Crew did an excellent job getting us parked without incident but that seems like a situation with a high potential for a negative outcome. Although a negative outcome was avoided, it may be beneficial to have a note in the SIP to let Crews know that the Marshaler and Wing Walker cannot see each other at a certain point in the parking process. I don't know if this is a common issue at every gate, but I always thought they could see each other the entire time.
1763608: The Pilot Flying (PF) was flying the LINKK1 arrival to ILS 27 at IAH. The PF initiated a VNAV descent on the LINKK1 and was below path during the arrival. Inside of RDFSH while in VNAV we were cleared for the ILS 27. 1500' was called for and set in MCP. Since we were in VNAV and the step downs were in the legs page, I agreed with this altitude in the MCP. Just inside TRANN the PF asked for approach mode, this disengaged VNAV and since we were below the VNAV path we continued to 1500 no longer protected to 2000' at DENTO or FESTA. We were VMC the entire time and had the airport ad runway insight. ATC issued a low altitude warning. We climbed to 2000' and completed the approach normally.
1763615: While descending on the RNAV ARRIVAL within a mile or two of waypoint ZZZZZ the autopilot, for unknown reasons, went into a degraded mode. While in the degraded mode the aircraft continued straight ahead at ZZZZZ not staying on the LNAV course. By the time we recognized the situation and got the autopilot out of the degraded mode the controller informed us we had missed the turn and he gave us a heading. Flight continued normally from there. I was the flying pilot. We were arriving on the RNAV STAR into ZZZ. At the time of the incident we were between the ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 waypoints, very close to the ZZZZZ waypoint. ATC instructed us to descend. The autopilot was engaged. I pushed the MCP FLCH button to start the decent. Immediately afterward I expected the aircraft to pull the power back and start a descent via the FLCH mode. Immediately the aircraft showed an 'autopilot mode' caution message on the ECAIS. Both the captain and I then realized that the aircraft was not descending as per the selected mode. We did not get a horn or a red autopilot warning message. Also the PFD showed that the autopilot was still engaged via the A/P FMA but the aircraft was not descending. We weren't sure if the aircraft was connected to the autopilot or not as per the conflicting information the aircraft was indicating. We then noticed that the aircraft airspeed was slowing and wasn't descending. I disconnected the autopilot and pushed the throttles forward to correct the low airspeed and pushed the yoke forward to start the aircraft descent. We also disconnected and reengaged the flight directors. We then noticed that the yellow 'autopilot mode' caution message had disappeared. Since we believed that the problem had been resolved I reengaged the autopilot. At that time the aircraft continued to descend and fly at the correct assigned airspeed. We didn't however notice that LNAV had not reengaged since we had just reengaged the autopilot and believed that all the modes had been reengaged correctly via the autopilot. At this time, only about 10 seconds later, we noticed that the aircraft was not tracking the arrival course correctly and immediately turned to the left towards the FMC arrival course to intercept. About 5 seconds later ATC said 'it appears that you missed your turn', and the gave us a 090 heading. The captain told ATC that we were having autopilot issues and were already correcting back to the STAR arrival course. We were then given two more heading changes. We followed ATC directions for the remainder of the approach and landing to a safe landing with no further incident. I'm not certain, but I may have accidentally pushed the autopilot disengage bar while I was reaching for the FLCH button to start the descent.
1763634: Got too low flaps warning on short final. Flap indicator showed Flaps 25. Flap handle was in landing flaps position. Recycled to no effect. Airspeed was below max flap speed. Aircraft was on safe path and speed for landing. Considered go-around with First Officer but concluded the safest action since all other parameters we stable, was to continue. We continued the approach and landed normally in touchdown zone with normal rollout without event. Flaps operated properly on ground.
1763654: In the logbook and on our flight plan we had MEL 27-88-02 which was suppose to deactivate the Kruger flap system. The logbook was reviewed and the MEL was discussed between the First Officer and myself. All the placards were in place and signed off by maintenance that the DMP was accomplished. We started the aircraft and taxied out to the runway. I did notice a Kruger light on the SFPI, which was in the MEL that it might be displayed. We took off and climbed out. As we retracted the slats we received an ECAM warning and a single chime. The First Office was flying so I handled the ECAM. The ECAM message showed a Kruger not retracted and a notation of MAX SPD 300KIAS/.65. We did our after takeoff flows and checklist and I told the First Officer to fly the airplane and to not exceed the speed shown in the notation on ECAM. I did remember that besides getting the Kruger light that you could also get an ECAM message saying Kruger Fault. This was not the message we received after bringing up the flaps. I decided to get Maintenance Control on the line with Dispatch. I queried the maintenance people about our situation. I explained what we were showing and that it did not correspond with the MEL we had in the log book. We both concluded that if we could we would continue .65/300 knots. Maintenance was sure that the MEL was complied with and that it was probably an erroneous message, but to be safe we would comply with the speeds on the ECAM. After a discussion with dispatch about extra fuel burn and a longer duration flight we decided we were safe even if the Kruger Flap was extended. The dispatcher did run the numbers for fuel burn with Kruger Flap extended. The flight was uneventful and we landed with no further problems. I did make a comment in the logbook about what had transpired during the flight so if this was an anomaly maintenance could add this message to the MEL. We exited the aircraft where I noticed the Kruger Flap on the left side of the aircraft was partially extended. I immediately got the mechanics involved and told them of the situation. We headed to hotel for a 3 hour layover where we were to return to fly later. After returning to the gateway, and heading to the same aircraft we noticed the gear doors down and a panel on the wing root open. I met up with the maintenance people and asked if there was a problem. He told me that the aircraft was out of service. I asked him what was going on and we were told that the DMP for the KRUGER Flap MEL had not been complied with even though it had been stated so in the log book. Our flight was eventually cancelled as they were having some issues with the log book and could not do the DMP for this MEL. The aircraft had MEL 27-88-02. During initial climb we received an ECAM for kruger flap not retracted. The MEL did not mention this warning so we complied with the restrictions and called dispatch and maintenance to see if they had any additional information for us and if they preferred us to come back or continue to our destination. Maintenance and the crew felt safe continuing to destination using the restrictions for the ECAM message and dispatch agreed.
1763656: Received communication from Operations that flight ZZZ to ZZZ1 was coming back to [the] gate because a customer had O2 oxygen tanks not approved for flying. Went onboard to investigate customer who was traveling with her infant. The oxygen bottles were for the infant. I asked if the baby could fly without oxygen. Customer assured me that yes, the baby could fly, the oxygen was for tonight at bed time when she arrived in ZZZ1. I advised customer of our policy and that these canisters could not fly. Customer advised me that both she and the baby and the oxygen all flew in from ZZZ2. I relayed our policy and advised her that I would take the oxygen down to baggage claim area. Passenger had two full canisters in a black roller board bag, and the 3rd O2 container was in a small pouch with a shoulder strap that easily looked like a shoulder strap purse. The CSR boarding the aircraft was senior and did not notice any discrepancies that may have alerted her to the fact that there was oxygen canisters being transported. Once the plane pushed off the jet bridge the flight attendant onboard witnessed the customer with the O2 bottle and inquired about it. Baggage Service is advised and has customer's phone contact, but bottles cannot be flown, customer will need to make arrangements in ZZZ1 for the babies oxygen tonight. Will also follow up with a report on how the oxygen canisters made it through TSA in ZZZ2 undetected.
1763673: Small airport with a horrible FBO. No line help or marshaling. Got distracted on the walk around by pulling chocks and passengers trying to find his ID. No GPU, so we were rushing to get the engines running to cool down the cabin with pax. Got everything running and programmed. Went to taxi out and realized that the nose gear pin was still disconnected. Shut down the left so FO can jump out and put it back in. We get the pin in, he sits down, start to taxi out again. 7 small aircraft in the traffic pattern and 4 on the taxiway around us, so both of our heads were outside watching for traffic. None of the checklists or flows, after start, have you look at the engines until you set takeoff power. So we accomplished the 'Before Takeoff' checklist, received a 'Takeoff OK'. Took the runway, held the breaks, go to set takeoff power and the left engine is still off. We quickly asked ATC for a short delay on the runway, started the left engine, and made sure everything was ready and all checklist were complete. We were able to depart without any issues. We noticed that the steering was not responsive. Got distracted on the walk around and when being rushed, the nose pin was missed. That led to shutting the left engine down. Shut down the left engine and sent the FO out to put the pin back in. Just need to slow down and pay attention better. And not having any line service made the situation more difficult and rushed. If we had a marshaler, they may have been able to bring our attention to the nose wheel not connected when they removed the chocks. But at the end of the day, it still was my responsibility to make sure it was in.
1763676: I did two flights both returning from the north. IFR route to ZZZ vectors to ILS Runway XXR with the heading toward ZZZZZ about 150 degrees at 5500 ft. As I recall on both approaches at about 3 miles from ZZZZ, coming from the north, on a heading of 150 I was assigned a 180 heading and 4000 ft. Inside of 3 miles I was assigned 250 heading and descent to 3800 ft., maintain 3800 ft. until established, then cleared for the approach.Because the turn is originating so close to ZZZZ, the aircraft has to turn more than 100 degrees to intercept the final approach course. This puts the aircraft in a roll AOB (Angle of Bank) of at least 30 degrees. This is a steep AOB for a Medevac flight, the crews are typically working on the patient. The turn also puts us inside ZZZZ, before ZZZZ3.This vector also puts us above the glide slope, from 4000 ft. to the glide path the aircraft needs to descend 400 ft. in less than a minute and continue that descent at 500 fpm to be on glide path. This puts the aircraft at almost a 1000 fpm descent just to get to the glide slope and then adjust to 500 fpm to continue on course and on glide slope all occurring within about 2 minutes. The distance from ZZZZ to the final approach fix is 4.3 miles and the aircraft would need to descend from 4000 ft. to 2500 ft. at 90 kts. in about 3 minutes. My point, it is aggressive and in my opinion not necessary to put us in that position. As a general rule glide slope should not be intercepted from above. This type of profile forces us to slow down and have a rapid rate of descent, this can cause an unstable approach. This vector profile is a recurring trend for TRACON controllers. I have addressed this many times with the supervisors and directly with the controllers as its occurring. Controllers have cited there is a MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) in that area and they can't get us lower or there is 'a lot of traffic'. I am well aware of the MVA and TERPS (Terminal Instrument Approach Procedures). What I don't understand is why can't the controllers vector us at 4000 ft. and closer to ZZZZ2, or between ZZZZ and ZZZZ2, before turning us onto the localizer and glide slope? There is a feeder route on the initial approach from ZZZZ1 (Initial Approach Fix) to ZZZZ2 at 4200 ft. This is in the sector that we are arriving from the north, but the controllers will not use the higher altitude and vector closer to ZZZZ2 before turning us onto the localizer. Also the initial approach segment between ZZZZ2 and ZZZZ goes from 4200 ft. to 3600 ft., yet the controllers never put us at 3600 ft. prior to ZZZZ within the TERP of the approach. Filing a flight plan to ZZZZ1 or ZZZZ2 IAP has no effect, controllers just disregard and vector as stated.
1763678: Throughout the arrival ATC requested best forward speed, comply at ZZZZZ: 230kts, 10,000 ft. After ZZZZZ, we were vectored for the approach to XXL. We called the airport in sight and ATC cleared us for the approach. We were also requested to slow to 160kts for spacing with an aircraft in front of us for the same runway. At this point I had flaps 8, and requested flaps 20. [Another] flight was also being vectored for XXL, coming from the west. ATC then asked us to slow to final approach speed and if we had the aircraft ahead insight. We did not have it insight, so were quickly told to turn left to a heading of 270. I believe the [other] flight was then cleared for the approach ahead of us, behind the first aircraft we were following. They then gave us a right turn back to the East and told us to intercept the localizer for XXL, but we were 90 degrees to the course and wouldn't have been able to make it and we weren't configured. I think I remember the controller stating that 'this isn't going to work' and asked if we could accept runway XXR. We said yes, and ATC began vectoring us for XXR. At this point I was very task saturated and should've done a go around. I was very concerned that the aircraft was set up for XXR and verbalized this. He said it was. In hindsight, I should have just disconnected the autopilot. We were configured by the FAF and a stable approach was completed. A go around should have been executed before this situation got so far. We did not have time to find the original aircraft in front of us, and then the [other] flight was thrown into the situation. When ATC switched us to XXR, a localizer frequency should have been offered. The Captain called the tower after we landed to discuss what happened with the supervisor. He said they were happy he called, and the supervisor was watching the whole situation. He also agreed a report should be completed. After being vectored on to final for runway XXL from the west at on approach control frequency, I called the airport in sight after we descended below the clouds, approximately 3,000 ft. AGL, ATC cleared us for the visual approach and instructed a speed reduction to 160 KIAS. There was another aircraft on final about 4 miles ahead of us. I offered to slow to approach speed and the controller immediately requested for us to do so while asking if we could also see the aircraft ahead of us. I indicated that I was unable to see an aircraft ahead. First Officer already had flaps 8 and called for flaps 20 to start slowing when I replied that I was unable to see the other aircraft. Suddenly ATC issued instructions for us to turn left to a heading of 270. At the same time, [another] flight was cleared to join the localizer ahead from the opposite direction, from the east, and midway between us and the previous aircraft. As we rolled out on the 270 heading, we were instructed to turn back to the right to a heading of 090 to intercept the localizer. As we rolled through 360 I could clearly see the [other] aircraft, rolling onto final about 2 miles ahead of us. By then it appeared as if the controller was going to want us to join the LOC on almost a 90 degree angle, not fully configured on a 3 mile final. I was about to ask for re-sequence when the controller asked if I could take runway XXR. I responded that we could, without taking the time to consult the flying pilot. As we crossed the approach path for XXL I was quickly pulling up the LOC frequency for XXR and trying to get the frequencies retuned. [Pilot Flying] asked if I was sure it was XXR and not XXC. I followed procedure and got verification from ATC prior to tuning it on the RTU (Radio Tuning Unit). This seemed to take longer than [Pilot Flying] had expected and I was not yet fully aware of his level of stress over the sudden unnecessary changes. We were then vectored through the XXR LOC and given right turns back towards the airport and cleared for a visual to XXR. The approach and landing was stabilized and without further incident. In retrospect, I think not giving [Pilot Flying] time to give his input about accepting a different runway, understandably added to his stress. While I may not have been uncomfortable with what I saw outside the window, I could have made my fellow pilot less comfortable by not asking him what he was thinking. Other contributory factors were compounded when the controller did not offer a LOC frequency whilst changing runways after getting us to less than optimal airspeed and giving us an impromptu tour of his airspace. Our company procedures require us to use an ILS as a backup whenever available, even in visual conditions. This meant that our crew had to simultaneously deal with clarification of communications, following ATC instructions, practice slow flight, and setting up navigation for a late runway change. To add to the equation, there were 80 souls in the main cabin who were certainly wondering why we were zig-zagging around the airport. I think most pilots don't like being loaded up that much in the simulator. Even less do we enjoy such practice in a real airplane at low altitude, and in the most critical phase of flight. Once at the gate, I asked the tower for a phone number to Approach and was given the number that connected me immediately to the supervisor who had been standing behind the controller during the entire ordeal. ATC stated first that he was glad I called. He then explained to me that he had told the controller to re-sequence us and not try to save the situation after his first mistake had put us in a position for an unstable approach. He apologized for the inconvenience and indicated that the [other] aircraft should not have been squeezed into the line. He should have sent the [other] aircraft to runway XXR to begin with. But by the time the situation had developed, it was better for us to break off of the approach than toattempt to turn the other aircraft around. [The supervisor] was professional and wanted to reassure me that such traffic management is not acceptable and that the controller at the helm during the situation was made well aware of that fact. He and I agreed that a report should be filed if it has the potential prevent at least some similar situations from occurring. I can't speak for the ATC practices and procedures, but from my perspective, there are a few variables at play here that should receive a little more focus in the near future. This applies several large class B airports facilities as well warrants adequate and candid discussion. This applies several large class B airports facilities as well warrants adequate and candid discussion. RNAV arrivals have been created to help reduce controller and pilot work load as well as simplify clearance delivery. Issue them, let us all fly them as published, line us up, and watch us keep the line moving as you switch us to the next sector. Trust us to do our part as pilots. TCAS tells us how far behind the next aircraft we are. You want separation, ask us to keep 4 to 5 miles and we will do it. We will be far less confused and take up less time on frequency getting clarification of what you actually need us to do. Keeping the frequency more clear will also allow for us confused pilots to actually ask for the help we need when we don't understand something rather than have to wait for a lengthy exchange while a potentially adverse situation gets worse. It would also be nice if there were some regularly scheduled meetings between professional pilot groups and ATC groups. Before 9/11, it was as easy as asking on the radio if we could come visit the tower in between flights. But after all the bureaucrats got involved, common sense seemed to get tossed right out the window and now we have a generation of pilots who have never been to an ATC facility, seen a radar screen, or had the chance to ask questions directly to a controller and vice versa! I would love to see that decision get more attention.
1763685: The APU was deferred and I was the Pilot Flying on this leg. While descending through FL180, as Captain activated the exterior lights, I observed numerous fluctuations in my EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System) screens followed by a loss of the Flight Director, seed tape and information on my EHSI (Electronic Horizontal Situation Indicator). At that time, I lost my CDU as well as many of the ambient and indicating lights in the flight deck area. The upper EICAS screen began listing numerous amber messages. Captain determined that the aircraft had a Right AC Bus failure. Due to the loss of some indicating information on my flight instruments, I transferred aircraft control to Captain and he called for the R AC BUS OFF Non-normal Checklist. As I worked through the checklist, ATC cleared us for the ILSXXR approach. At the completion of that checklist electrical function had been restored. The upper EICAS screen only displayed an amber R UTIL BUS OFF message. Captain then called for the R UTIL BUS OFF Checklist. While resetting the R Utility Bus switch the Right Bus Tie tripped again and the partial loss of indicating instruments and lighting reoccurred. Per the R AC BUS OFF non-normal checklist, the Right Bus Tie may only be reset once in flight. The Captain and I agreed landing in the current condition was the best option. The flight was completed with no further issues.
1763723: While in climb to FL410 we were given a turn 20 degrees left for traffic. Passing through 36,600 feet Controller said a mistake had been made and descend to FL360. As we were descending Controller gave us a right turn to 110. At that time we received an RA which we followed to 35,500 before we were clear of conflict. We then climbed back to FL360 and reported our altitude and RA event to ATC. ATC stated there was confusion between two controller's plans. The controllers [should be] on the same page. What happened today isn't a surprise to me. Since the reduction in staffing of the controllers from the COVID-19 pandemic flying has been miserable and less safe. Most controllers are controlling several frequencies and are overloaded. We have had more TA's in the last 2 months than the last 3 years.
